This page reports a measurement project in cryptography — the mathematics of encryption. A 2026 research paper, PQShield-IoT, proposed a framework to protect Internet of Things (IoT) devices against future quantum computers, but supported its design with simulated numbers rather than real measurements. This project rebuilt the paper's cryptographic core and measured all of it for real: how fast the new algorithms run, how much data they force onto the network, whether their timing leaks secrets, and how the results change on the tiny chips IoT devices actually use. Every measurement points to the single sentence below — the thesis this entire page defends.

On CPU-class hardware, post-quantum cryptography costs almost nothing in time — its real cost is bytes on the wire. Computation only becomes binding at microcontroller class, and even there only for signing-heavy schemes.

Unpacked: on an ordinary laptop or server (a machine with a full CPU), switching to post-quantum cryptography barely slows anything down. What changes is size: the new methods need far more bytes to travel between the two devices, and for a battery-powered gadget sending data over a slow radio, every extra byte is the expensive part. Raw computing speed only becomes the bottleneck on a microcontroller, and even there only for the schemes that spend heavily on creating digital signatures.

What one key looks like to a tiny radio

The picture below makes the size problem visible. Each coloured cell is one radio frame of IEEE 802.15.4, the low-power radio many IoT devices use — roughly 100 usable bytes per frame. The rows compare how many frames it takes to send one public key or one digital signature, plus one full handshake in the hybrid style deployed by modern web browsers. Today's classical objects fit inside a single frame with room to spare; every post-quantum object shatters into many.

AnalogyA classical key is a postcard: it fits in one envelope and travels in one go. A post-quantum key is a parcel that the postal service forces you to cut into 8 postcard-sized pieces — or 25 for a signature — mail separately, and reassemble at the other end. Every piece can be lost in transit, every piece must be paid for, and on a battery-powered device the postage is battery life.
What one public key / signature looks like to an IoT radio — each cell ≈ one 802.15.4 frame (~100 B usable payload)
X25519 public key †32 B — fits with room to spare
ECDH P-256 public key †65 B — still one frame
Falcon-512 signature~655 B — 7 frames
ML-KEM-512 public key800 B — 8 frames
ML-DSA-44 signature2,420 B — 25 frames
Hybrid-768 handshake, total2,474 B — the whole exchange
classical († = breakable by a quantum computer — Shor's algorithm, § 1) post-quantum hybrid exchange

Compute tells the opposite story: ML-KEM-512's key-agreement step is as fast as optimised ECDH on the same machine, so the frames above are not paid for in processor time. Size, not speed, is what post-quantum cryptography charges an IoT device — and because radio transmission, not computation, is what drains a small device's battery, each extra frame is ultimately paid in battery life.

Five headline numbers

Five results carry the whole argument. They are previewed here and each is earned, step by step, in the numbered sections that follow.

In plain EnglishWhat the five tiles say, one by one:
  • Tile 1 — speed. Encapsulation is the step where one device wraps up a fresh shared secret for another. The new post-quantum method (ML-KEM-512) does it in the same fraction of a millisecond as ECDH, today's heavily optimised classical champion, on the same machine. Quantum safety costs essentially no extra time here.
  • Tile 2 — insurance. Running the old method and the new method together (the hybrid), so that an attacker must break both, adds only 64 bytes to the entire conversation. Belt and braces, nearly free.
  • Tile 3 — leaks. We built a deliberately careless password-tag check and watched it leak its secret through timing alone — a side channel — then confirmed that the security-critical post-quantum decapsulation step is constant-time, showing no such leak.
  • Tile 4 — the sharpest critique. Working backwards from real chip measurements, the base paper's four timing claims could only all be true if its single declared processor ran at four different clock speeds at once — between 25 and 189 MHz. No processor does that, so those numbers cannot be genuine measurements of the declared device.
  • Tile 5 — proof over promise. Every security claim made for this project's own handshake is checked by an automated test, and all eight pass — including that tampering is detected and safely rejected.

§ 0The whole story in plain words

This section tells the entire project as a story, assuming no background at all. Every idea here reappears later with full technical depth; if you read nothing else, read this.

Encryption is the quiet service you use hundreds of times a day. When you check a bank balance, send a private message, or when a smart meter on a wall reports a reading, the data is scrambled before it leaves the device so that anyone eavesdropping on the network sees only noise. Two devices can only unscramble each other's messages if they share a secret key — and that raises the founding puzzle of the field: how do two machines that have never met agree on a secret while talking over a wire everyone can listen to?

The answer, invented in the 1970s, is public-key cryptography. Each device owns a matched pair of keys — one it publishes to the world, one it keeps secret — arranged so that what the public half locks, only the private half unlocks. Strangers can now establish a shared secret in the open, and once they have it they switch to a much faster symmetric cipher for the actual conversation. Every secure connection you make works this way: a brief public-key opening, then fast symmetric encryption for the bulk of the data.

AnalogyPublic-key cryptography is a padlock and its key. I can mail open padlocks (my public key) to anyone in the world — I do not care who sees or copies them. You snap one shut around your message and post it back. Only I hold the key that opens my padlocks, so only I can read it — even though we never met to whisper a secret.

Quantum computers threaten exactly the padlock part. The security of every deployed padlock scheme — RSA, elliptic-curve exchange, the algorithms behind nearly every padlock icon in a browser — rests on two mathematical problems that ordinary computers would need longer than the age of the universe to solve. In 1994 Peter Shor showed that a large enough quantum computer solves both quickly. Not slightly faster: the problems collapse from practically impossible to routine, and making the keys bigger does not help. The symmetric ciphers, by contrast, survive almost untouched — a quantum computer speeds up brute-force guessing only modestly, and doubling the key size restores full strength. So the repair plan for all of cryptography is lopsided: replace the padlocks, keep the fast ciphers.

"We will upgrade when quantum computers arrive" does not work, because an adversary can record your encrypted traffic today, store it cheaply, and unscramble it the day the capability arrives — a strategy called harvest-now-decrypt-later, like steaming open a filing cabinet of sealed letters years after they were posted. For anything that must stay confidential for a decade — medical data, industrial telemetry, firmware — the deadline has effectively already passed. IoT makes this acute: a smart meter installed today may run 10–20 years without a single cryptographic upgrade. The cryptography it ships with is the cryptography it dies with.

Replacements exist — but they are bulky. After a multi-year worldwide competition, NIST published the first post-quantum standards in August 2024. The new schemes rest on different mathematics — chiefly lattices, grids of points in hundreds of dimensions where finding short paths is believed hard even for quantum machines. They are believed safe, and (as this project measures) they are surprisingly fast. But their keys and signatures are ten to a hundred times larger than the classical ones: 800 bytes where 32 used to do, 2,420-byte signatures against radio frames that carry about 100 bytes each. On a laptop broadband link that is nothing; on a battery-powered sensor whispering over a low-power radio, it is the whole problem.

Enter the base paper. PQShield-IoT, published in 2026, proposes a complete protocol framework for quantum-safe IoT: post-quantum key establishment, device identities recorded on a blockchain instead of a central authority, firmware integrity checks, and an optimisation layer. Its architectural choices are largely sound. But every one of its performance figures comes from simulation, and the paper never explains how those numbers were produced — no hardware named for the timing runs, no methodology, no variance. A simulation only reproduces what its author builds into it; it cannot surprise you. The paper's numbers are, in the strict sense, unattributable: there is no way to tell what was measured, on what, or how.

This project measured everything for real. Sixteen encryption and signature schemes were benchmarked on real hardware with a defended methodology; a working hybrid handshake was built over a live network connection and its byte counts audited exactly; timing leaks were hunted with statistics; and published cycle-accurate measurements of the very same code running on a real microcontroller were used to bridge from the desktop to the device class the paper targets. The verdict is the thesis at the top of this page: the new cryptography's latency cost on normal hardware is close to zero; its real cost is message size — bandwidth, and the battery drained by transmitting. The paper's optimisation layer polishes the resource that was never the bottleneck at its own device class.

And one finding cuts deeper. Checking the paper's four published crypto timings against real, published chip measurements of the same code shows they are mutually inconsistent: for all four to be genuine measurements, the paper's single declared 120 MHz processor would have to have run at four different speeds — from 25 MHz to 189 MHz — at once. It is like four stopwatches timing one runner and reporting four different races. That does not prove bad faith; it proves the numbers came from some unstated model rather than from the declared device — which is precisely why measurement, with methodology stated, matters. This project also found a security-relevant contradiction: the paper claims forward secrecy — the property that yesterday's recorded traffic stays safe even if a device's key is stolen tomorrow — while using permanent, reusable keys that forfeit exactly that property. The handshake built here uses fresh keys per connection and demonstrates the difference rather than asserting it.

Read straight through, or dip in anywhere: each section restates what it needs.

§ 1Why quantum computers break today's cryptography

Almost every secure connection made today rests on two mathematical problems being hard: integer factorisation, which underpins RSA, and the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm, which underpins ECDH, ECDSA, X25519 and Ed25519 — essentially all of the modern padlock layer. Shor's algorithm (1994) solves both in polynomial time on a large enough quantum computer — not “somewhat faster”, but a shift from intractable to easy. No larger key size saves them, because the attack scales polynomially.

Two kinds of cryptography — and only one is in danger

To see why that sentence matters, separate the two jobs cryptography does. The first job is bulk protection: scrambling the actual data. Symmetric ciphers such as AES do this, both sides using one shared secret key, and they are blisteringly fast. The second job is the hard one: getting that shared key to two parties who have never met, over a channel anyone can tap, and proving identity while doing so. That is the public-key layer — key agreement (ECDH, X25519) and digital signatures (RSA, ECDSA, Ed25519).

The public-key layer works because of a beautiful asymmetry: some mathematical operations are easy to do and monstrously hard to undo. Multiplying two enormous prime numbers takes a microsecond; recovering those primes from the product (integer factorisation — the problem RSA rests on) is believed to take an ordinary computer longer than the universe has existed. Likewise, on an elliptic curve it is easy to compute the point Q = kP from a secret number k, and believed infeasible to recover k from P and Q (the discrete logarithm problem — what ECDH, ECDSA, X25519 and Ed25519 rest on). Classically, the best attacks on both problems grow sub-exponentially or exponentially with key size, so a 2048-bit RSA key or a 256-bit curve sits comfortably out of reach.

In plain EnglishCryptography has a fast workhorse (symmetric ciphers — one shared key, both ends) and a clever front door (public-key methods — how strangers get that shared key in the first place). The front door is built from maths that is easy forwards and practically impossible backwards. Quantum computers break the front door, not the workhorse.

Shor and Grover: what a quantum computer actually changes

A quantum computer is not simply a faster laptop. Built from qubits, it runs a different kind of algorithm — and for most tasks it offers no advantage at all. Its danger to cryptography comes from exactly two algorithms, and the difference between them dictates everything that follows.

Shor's algorithm attacks the structure of the front-door problems directly. It solves integer factorisation and the discrete logarithm in polynomial time — the moment a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists, RSA, ECDH, ECDSA, X25519 and Ed25519 all fail completely. Crucially, you cannot buy safety with a bigger key: because the attack's cost grows only polynomially with key size, doubling the key inconveniences the attacker instead of stopping them. The trapdoor these schemes depend on simply stops being a trapdoor.

Grover's algorithm is the other quantum algorithm people cite, and it is far milder. It searches an unstructured space of size N in about √N steps — a quadratic speedup on brute-force search, nothing like Shor's collapse. Its effect on a symmetric cipher is to halve the effective key length: AES-128 drops to roughly 64-bit security (too weak to trust), but AES-256 keeps ~128 bits and remains strong. Grover also parallelises poorly, so its real-world advantage is even smaller than the theory suggests.

AnalogyGrover is a safecracker who can somehow try combinations two at a time — worrying, but answered by adding more dials to the safe. Shor is the discovery that the safe's whole locking mechanism has a hidden resonance that reveals the combination outright — and adding dials barely slows him down. You retire that model of safe; you do not buy a bigger one.

That asymmetry — one layer annihilated, the other merely bruised — dictates the entire migration strategy, and both the base paper and this project follow it:

Design ruleReplace the public-key parts (key exchange, signatures). Keep the symmetric parts — AES-256-GCM for bulk encryption, SHA3-256 for key derivation — with big keys.

That is why AES-256-GCM and SHA3-256 (a hash function, used here to derive keys) appear unchanged throughout this project: against Grover they simply have security to spare.

In plain EnglishQuantum computers bring exactly two relevant tricks. One (Shor) totally breaks the maths behind today's key exchange and signatures, and bigger keys cannot fix it. The other (Grover) only halves the strength of the scrambling ciphers, which is fixed by using 256-bit keys. So the plan everywhere — this project included — is: swap out the key-exchange and signature layer, keep AES-256 and SHA3 as they are.

Harvest now, decrypt later

A fair objection: quantum computers at Shor scale do not exist yet, so why act now? Because encrypted traffic does not expire. An adversary can record ciphertext today, store it for pennies, and decrypt it the day the capability arrives. Interception is passive and cheap; storage is cheaper every year; only the final decryption step waits on hardware that does not yet exist. For any data whose confidentiality must outlive the arrival of that hardware — medical records, industrial control telemetry, diplomatic traffic, firmware images — the protection deadline is set by the attacker's future capability, and for long-lived secrets it has already passed.

AnalogyImagine an adversary photocopying every sealed letter that passes through the post office — unable to open any of them today, but filing them all away. Years later someone invents a way to steam open that brand of envelope. Every letter in the archive opens at once, retroactively. Recording encrypted traffic now and waiting for a quantum computer is exactly that filing cabinet.

IoT feels this hardest. A smart meter, pipeline sensor or implanted medical device deployed today may run for 10–20 years, often without ever receiving a cryptographic upgrade — many such devices cannot be updated at all once installed. The cryptography shipped in the firmware is the cryptography the device dies with. A device installed in 2026 with quantum-broken key exchange is not “fine until quantum computers arrive”; every message it ever sends is already harvestable.

In plain EnglishYou do not need a quantum computer today to be a quantum threat today — recording scrambled traffic now and unscrambling it later is enough. Devices that live for twenty years on their factory software must therefore ship quantum-safe cryptography now, which is why this problem is urgent for IoT in particular.

Why IoT is the hard case

Post-quantum cryptography is not free: its keys, ciphertexts and signatures are much larger than classical ones, and some schemes are much slower. IoT is exactly where that hurts, for four compounding reasons:

  • Tiny compute. A typical constrained node is an ARM Cortex-M-class microcontroller running at tens of MHz — thousands of times slower than a laptop CPU. An operation that costs an invisible fraction of a millisecond on a desktop can cost hundreds of milliseconds, or minutes, there (§ 8 measures exactly this).
  • Tiny memory. Tens of kilobytes of RAM and hundreds of kilobytes of storage. Some post-quantum operations need more stack — working scratch space — than the entire device has RAM, which is a hard wall, not a slowdown.
  • Tiny radio frames. IEEE 802.15.4 — the radio underneath Zigbee, Thread and 6LoWPAN — carries a 127-byte physical frame, leaving roughly 100 bytes of usable payload after headers. A 2,420-byte post-quantum signature does not fit in a frame; it travels as about 25 fragments, every one of which can be lost, must be reassembled in order, and costs radio energy. Lose one fragment and the whole object must wait for a retransmission.
  • Battery. On these devices, transmitting over the radio usually costs far more energy than computing, so bytes-on-wire — not CPU cycles — is the real currency a designer must budget. This single fact is why the thesis at the top of this page is phrased in bytes.

So the IoT question is not “is post-quantum cryptography secure?” — as far as anyone knows, it is — but “does it fit, and what does it cost?” That question is answerable only by measurement, which is exactly where the base paper falls short, and where this project contributes.

In plain EnglishIoT devices are slow, cramped, whisper over a radio in 100-byte gulps, and live on batteries where transmitting is the expensive act. Post-quantum cryptography is bulky, and some of it is slow. Whether the two fit together is a question about numbers — so someone has to actually measure them.

The NIST standards

The world's answer to Shor arrived through a multi-year NIST competition: dozens of candidate schemes, years of public attack attempts, and in August 2024 the first finished standards. The survivors rest on kinds of mathematics for which no efficient quantum algorithm is known. The table lists the five that matter to this project, including the two roles they fill: key encapsulation (agreeing on secret keys) and digital signatures (proving identity and integrity).

Standardisation status (as used in this project)
StandardNameFormerlyRoleBasis
FIPS 203 (Aug 2024)ML-KEMCRYSTALS-Kyberkey encapsulationmodule lattices (M-LWE)
FIPS 204 (Aug 2024)ML-DSACRYSTALS-Dilithiumsignaturesmodule lattices
FIPS 205 (Aug 2024)SLH-DSASPHINCS+signatureshash functions only
FIPS 206 (draft)FN-DSAFalconcompact signaturesNTRU lattices
selected Mar 2025HQC—backup KEMcodes (not lattices)

Three reading notes. First, the renames: the base paper (written against the pre-standard names) says Kyber512 and Dilithium2; the finished standards call the same designs ML-KEM-512 and ML-DSA-44, and this page uses both interchangeably. Second, the deliberate diversity: SLH-DSA rests only on hash functions — the most conservative assumption available — and HQC, selected in March 2025 as a backup KEM, is code-based rather than lattice-based, chosen precisely so that a breakthrough against lattices would not compromise every standardised KEM at once. Third, notice what that diversity means: NIST itself is hedging. It does not fully trust any single mathematical basket, however well studied.

Deployed systems hedge too. Modern TLS — the encryption under the web itself — now runs a hybrid key exchange by default in major browsers: a classical exchange and a post-quantum one, both feeding the session key. The base paper hedges at neither level, which becomes Gap 1 in § 3.

AnalogyA hybrid is two different locks on one door, and the door opens only when both are picked. A burglar who masters the old lock (a quantum computer breaking elliptic curves) still faces the new one; a burglar who finds a flaw in the new lock (a lattice breakthrough) still faces the old. You only lose if both fall — and the second lock, as § 6 measures, costs 64 bytes.
Cautionary tale — why hybrids existSIKE, a NIST candidate with beautifully small keys (built on isogenies — mappings between elliptic curves — a different mathematical basis again), was completely broken in 2022 by a classical attack (Castryck–Decru) — no quantum computer involved, keys recovered in about an hour on one ordinary core, after the scheme had survived years of public scrutiny. The lesson is that cryptographic confidence is not a guarantee, even for well-studied designs. NIST hedged by standardising the code-based HQC alongside lattice-based ML-KEM; deployed TLS hedges with hybrids. The base paper does not hedge at all — and its comparison table still cites SIKE as “quantum-resilient” (§ 3).
In plain EnglishThe replacements are real, finished, government-standardised algorithms with new names (ML-KEM for key agreement, ML-DSA and friends for signatures). But the standards body spread its bets across different kinds of maths, and the web's own encryption now runs old and new methods together — because one promising scheme, SIKE, was broken overnight by an ordinary computer after years of scrutiny. Prudence is the norm everywhere except, notably, in the base paper.

§ 2The base paper: PQShield-IoT

PQShield-IoT is an integrated architecture. Its authors did not invent a new piece of mathematics; their contribution is wiring several known pieces into one complete lifecycle for an IoT device: blockchain device identity → post-quantum key establishment → an encrypted session → auditable firmware updates. It appeared in a legitimate Springer journal (Iranian J. Sci. Technol. Trans. Electr. Eng. 50:203–221, SCIE and Scopus indexed), which matters here: this project critiques a peer-reviewed publication, not an easy target.

In plain EnglishThe paper proposes a complete security system for smart devices. Every device gets an identity written into a shared, tamper-evident register; when two devices want to talk, they agree on a temporary secret code using quantum-resistant mathematics; the conversation itself is scrambled with a conventional, well-trusted cipher; and every software update leaves a permanent audit trail. This section unpacks each of those pieces in ordinary language, records exactly what the paper claims about their speed — four numbers you will need again in § 8 — and gives the paper honest credit for what it does well.

The building blocks, in plain language

Four pieces of vocabulary carry the whole design, so it is worth understanding each one before touching the cryptography.

A blockchain is, stripped of the hype, an append-only record book that many computers keep in sync: you can add a page, but you can never tear one out or alter an old one without everybody noticing, because each page carries a fingerprint of the page before it. PQShield-IoT uses a permissioned blockchain: unlike Bitcoin, strangers cannot join; only the network operator and its registered devices write to it. On this ledger live smart contracts — small programs that execute automatically when a valid request arrives, so admission decisions are made by code rather than by a clerk.

What gets registered is each device's firmware identity. A firmware hash is the output of a hash function applied to the device's entire software — a 32-byte fingerprint that changes completely if even one bit of the software is altered. Finally, an access-control list (ACL) is nothing more exotic than a guest list: a table of who may do what, consulted before any request is honoured.

Analogy — the identity layer as a gated communityThe permissioned blockchain is the town's land registry, written in ink with a carbon copy in every house — nobody can quietly rewrite history. The smart contract is the automated registry clerk who checks paperwork the same way every time and cannot be bribed. The firmware hash is a wax-seal impression of the device's software: if anyone tampers with the software, the seal no longer matches the one on file. And the ACL is the guest list at the gate — being registered is not the same as being allowed in everywhere.

The cryptographic core

The security engine combines four primitives, split along exactly the line that § 1 said quantum computers force. The public-key parts are replaced with post-quantum schemes; the symmetric parts are kept, with big keys:

  • Kyber512 as the KEM, i.e. the machinery that lets two devices agree a fresh secret across an open network. Its security rests on lattice problems, which no known quantum algorithm solves efficiently.
  • Dilithium2 for digital signatures — the stamps that prove a registration or update really came from the device it names.
  • AES-256-GCM for the encrypted session itself — a symmetric cipher, kept because Grover's algorithm only halves symmetric strength and 256-bit keys leave ample margin.
  • SHA3-256 as the KDF.

The session key is derived as (the paper's Eq. 5):

K_sess = KDF(ss ‖ ID ‖ ID′ ‖ T ‖ T′)

Read it as a recipe: the Kyber shared secret (ss) is blended together with both device identities (ID, ID′) and both timestamps (T, T′). Binding identity and time into the key is genuinely good practice: it gives every session a unique, fresh key and resists replay attacks, because a message keyed to yesterday's timestamp simply will not decrypt today. This project's own handshake in § 6 adopts the same idea. (Hold on to one detail for § 3, though: everything in that recipe except ss is public information — a fact that decides Gap 6.)

Analogy — padlock, box and blenderPublic-key crypto is a padlock you hand out freely while keeping the only key: anyone can snap it shut on a box, only you can open it. The KEM is exactly that — the sender locks a freshly invented secret in a box that only the receiver's private key opens. The KDF is then a blender: secret, names and dates go in, and out comes a smoothie (the session key) unique to this pair of devices at this moment. Change any ingredient — even the date — and you get a visibly different smoothie.

The identity and access layer

Rather than relying on a certificate authority, each device is registered on the permissioned blockchain at manufacture, carrying three things: a device ID, the firmware fingerprint SHA3-256(firmware), and a signing key. Registration is a signed transaction:

T_reg = ⟨ID_i, H_fw, pk_sig, σ_i, ts⟩

A smart contract verifies the signature and appends the record to the ledger. From then on, access control is a two-part check: the ACL says whether this device may do what it is asking, and the device's current firmware hash must match the one on file — so a device whose software has been tampered with fails authorisation automatically, even if its identity is genuine. Firmware updates are version-chained: each new firmware record points back to its parent, producing an auditable history rather than an overwrite. That chaining is a real defence against rollback attacks, because an attacker cannot silently resurrect an old, vulnerable firmware version — the chain records exactly which version is current.

An optimisation layer sits on top, with three ideas: algorithmic pruning (score each available primitive against the device's CPU, memory and bandwidth profile and pick the best fit), adaptive key rotation (rotate keys based on measured energy and throughput rather than a fixed schedule), and hardware acceleration (offload the heavy mathematics to a crypto co-processor).

In plain EnglishInstead of trusting a central certificate company, the network keeps its own tamper-evident register. A device is admitted only if its identity is on the register and the fingerprint of its software matches the fingerprint on file — so hacked devices lock themselves out. Updates never erase history; they add a new page that points at the old one, so you can always audit what ran when.

What it claims (all from simulation)

Every headline number in the paper comes from simulation — a software model of the devices and network, not measurements of physical hardware. The claims are broad and specific:

  • End-to-end latency of 50 ms; throughput of 20 operations per second.
  • Device registration under 250 ms even at scale (95 ms at 50 nodes, rising to 215 ms at 200); session establishment 110 ms → 265 ms across the same range.
  • Verification success ≥ 98.7%; energy 1.1–4.8 mJ per session; CPU utilisation under 50%.
  • A claimed 28.5% improvement in session integrity and a 33.3% throughput gain over its comparison baselines.

And then there is the paper's Table 6 — the per-operation cryptographic latencies. These four numbers are the ones this project later puts on trial against real silicon, so they deserve their own table:

Base paper Table 6 — claimed per-operation latencies
OperationClaimed latency
Kyber512 encapsulation28 ms
Kyber512 decapsulation31 ms
Dilithium2 sign42 ms
Dilithium2 verify36 ms
Remember these four numbers28 / 31 / 42 / 36. In § 8 they are tested against measured cycle counts of the very same code base running on real hardware — and they turn out to imply four different clock speeds for the paper's one declared device. Everything in that finding traces back to this table.
In plain EnglishThe paper says its system is fast, frugal and reliable — and gives precise-sounding figures for each cryptographic step. But all of them come from a software model, and (as § 3 shows) the paper never explains how the model turned computation into milliseconds. Precise-sounding is not the same as verifiable.

What is genuinely good about it

Fairness matters — in a viva, an examiner will respect balance far more than a hatchet job — and the paper earns real credit on four counts:

  • The integration is real. Many papers do post-quantum crypto or blockchain identity; this one wires identity → key establishment → encrypted session → audit into one coherent lifecycle, end to end.
  • The primitive choices are correct. Kyber512 and Dilithium2 are the right NIST Category 1/2 picks for constrained devices, and keeping AES-256-GCM and SHA3 is exactly what Grover's algorithm dictates. (How those primitives are used is a separate matter — see Gap 6.)
  • Firmware attestation is well-designed. Binding a firmware hash into registration and version-chaining updates is a genuinely good answer to rollback attacks.
  • The evaluation is broad — latency, energy, CPU, memory, throughput, ACL behaviour, and an ablation study of the optimiser, plus a comparison table against other frameworks.

The problem is not what it measures. It is how — which is where § 3 begins.

§ 3Six gaps — the project's roadmap

Each gap below comes from reading the paper closely — quoting its own section and table numbers — not from a review checklist. Each one maps to a phase of this project, and each ends in a measured number or a built artefact that closes it. Together they are the project plan.

In plain EnglishSix things are missing or wrong in the base paper, in everyday terms: (1) it relies on the new mathematics alone, with no classical backup lock; (2) its speed figures come with no explanation of how they were measured, so nobody can check them; (3) it picked one signature scheme without comparing the alternatives; (4) it never checked whether the implementation leaks secrets through how long operations take; (5) it never connects its simulated numbers to any real chip; and (6) it promises that past conversations stay safe even if a device's key is later stolen — while using a key-handling design that breaks exactly that promise.
Gap 1 → Phase 3

Pure PQC, no hybrid

PQShield-IoT establishes keys with Kyber alone. That is a defensible "clean" design — but it is out of step with how real migrations are actually being done. Deployed TLS 1.3 (Chrome, Firefox, Cloudflare) defaults to the hybrid group X25519MLKEM768: the session key is derived from both an X25519 exchange and an ML-KEM-768 encapsulation, like fitting a door with two different locks so a burglar must pick both.

Why hedge? Because lattice cryptanalysis is young compared to decades of RSA and elliptic-curve scrutiny — and because SIKE (§ 1) showed that a well-studied candidate can fall overnight to a purely classical attack. If lattices ever fall, every PQShield-IoT session key falls with them; a hybrid would still be protected by its classical leg, and against a future quantum computer by its post-quantum leg. It defends both directions at once.

The paper never asks the one question that would let a designer weigh this: what does hybrid actually cost? Phase 3 builds it and measures it — the answer (a few dozen bytes, sub-millisecond) turns "why hybrid?" into "why not?".

measured: +64 B, ~+0.6 ms
Gap 2 → Phases 2 & 5

Latencies with no methodology

This is the central gap, and it must be stated precisely, because the tempting sloppy version is falsifiable from the paper itself. The paper does use real cryptographic libraries: its §3.6 describes a co-simulation built on Contiki-NG (an operating system for tiny devices) and NS-3 (a network simulator), and explicitly names PQClean and liboqs. Claiming "no real library was used" would be false — an examiner can find that sentence in seconds.

The defensible gap is narrower and still decisive: the paper reports Table 6's latencies but never says how they were obtained. On what host did the crypto actually run? Not stated. The device is an emulated Cortex-M4F profile, not silicon — so the milliseconds must come from some mapping between host execution and the modelled device, and that mapping is never described. No cycle counts, no clock frequency for the timing model, no repetition counts, no variance. The numbers are unattributable: you cannot tell what was measured, on what, or how it was scaled.

Why it matters: a simulation reproduces only what its author programmed into it. If the model omits a behaviour — say, that Dilithium signing retries an unpredictable number of times (§ 5) — it reports a confident, wrong number. And there is a bonus: because the paper used PQClean, and pqm4 compiles the same PQClean source for the Cortex-M4, § 8's comparison is a same-codebase check — nobody can dismiss the discrepancy it finds as "different implementations".

measured: 16 schemes, full methodology
Gap 3 → Phase 2

One signature scheme, no comparison

The paper fixes on Dilithium2 and never compares alternatives — yet the three post-quantum signature families have wildly different shapes, and the differences are exactly the ones an IoT designer must trade off.

Falcon-512 produces signatures of roughly 655 bytes (variable-length) and verifies extremely fast, but signing is floating-point heavy and key generation is expensive. SPHINCS+ signs in seconds on a microcontroller and its signatures run to 8–17 KB, but its security rests only on hash functions, the most conservative assumption available.

For a constrained device the stakes are concrete: a signature 3.7× smaller (Falcon vs ML-DSA) can decide whether a signed firmware update fits the radio budget at all. Choosing one scheme without comparing is a design risk — Phase 2 benchmarks all three families for time and size, and § 8 maps them onto device classes.

measured: time and size, all three
Gap 4 → Phase 4

No side-channel analysis

The paper contains no timing analysis of any kind. A side channel is information escaping through a system's physical behaviour rather than its mathematics: like a safecracker who never forces the door but simply listens to the clicks of the dial. If an operation's running time depends on secret data, an attacker with a stopwatch learns the secret — however perfect the algebra.

This is not theoretical for these exact algorithms. The KyberSlash attacks (2023–24) recovered Kyber secret keys because reference decapsulation performed a division whose timing depended on secret data; the reference code and PQClean were patched. And ML-KEM's chosen-ciphertext security specifically depends on its implicit-rejection path — on a bad ciphertext, decapsulation must silently return a decoy value in exactly the same time as the honest path — being implemented in constant time.

A framework that deploys ML-KEM without checking this has an unexamined attack surface. Phase 4 both demonstrates a timing leak you can watch happen and verifies that the deployed decapsulation path is clean.

measured: leak shown, decaps clean
Gap 5 → Phase 5

No bridge to real hardware

Even granting the simulation on its own terms, nothing in the paper connects its numbers to any published measurement of real constrained hardware — despite pqm4 existing precisely to provide community-verified cycle counts for these algorithms on real ARM Cortex-M4 chips, compiled from the same PQClean source the paper's toolchain names.

Nor does the paper offer any guidance on which scheme suits which class of device. That question has a standard vocabulary: RFC 7228 classifies constrained devices by memory, and a useful framework should say where its recommendations stop applying. Phase 5 builds both missing pieces: a desktop-to-device extrapolation anchored in pqm4's real-silicon cycle counts, and a scheme-to-device-class recommendation matrix.

built: pqm4 bridge + device matrix
Gap 6 — the sharpest

Forward secrecy claimed, not provided

This one sits squarely inside the cryptography, and it is arguably the sharpest critique in the whole analysis. Forward secrecy is the promise that compromising a long-term key today must not expose sessions recorded yesterday — and it is achieved by using ephemeral keys, generated per session and destroyed afterwards.

What the paper claims: §4.9 states that "Kyber512, Dilithium2 achieve forward secrecy and long-term resistance to quantum attacks". What the protocol does: §3.2 states that "every device maintains a pre-computed post-quantum key pair for both encryption and signing", and its Eq. 2 encapsulates against that long-term key. There is no ephemeral KEM keypair anywhere in the protocol.

That is a contradiction, not a nuance. With a static KEM key, an attacker who ever obtains sk_kem — via a stolen device, a firmware dump, a court order — can decapsulate the ciphertext of every recorded session and recover every session key. Eq. 5's KDF does not rescue it: the extra ingredients (IDs, timestamps) are all public, so they add freshness but no secrecy. This is precisely the harvest-now-decrypt-later scenario the entire post-quantum field exists to prevent — reintroduced by key management, on a framework whose title promises quantum resilience.

The contrast is a free win for this project: the Phase 3 handshake (§ 6) generates fresh X25519 and fresh ML-KEM keypairs for every single run, so it does provide forward secrecy — demonstrable in code, not asserted in prose. A related, softer point: §3.2 also claims the design is "eliminating vulnerability to man-in-the-middle attackers". Signing the exchange does give authentication, but "eliminating" is a strong word for a paper with no security model, no proof, and no analysis of the on-chain key lookup as the actual trust anchor. That is an overclaim in wording — raised as such, not as a break.

demonstrated by contrast
Analogy — why static keys break the forward-secrecy promise (Gap 6)Imagine posting sealed letters for years, all secured by the one lock whose only key lives in your desk drawer. A patient thief does not need to open anything now — he simply photocopies every sealed envelope as it passes through the mail and files the copies away. The day he finally steals the drawer key, the entire archive opens at once: every letter you ever sent, back to the first. Writing the date and the recipient's name on each envelope (the paper's KDF garnish of IDs and timestamps) changes nothing — those are written on the outside, visible to the thief all along. Forward secrecy is the opposite discipline: a brand-new lock for every letter, its key melted down the moment the letter is read. Steal the drawer then, and you hold nothing that opens anything old.

What else close reading found

Four further observations came out of the same close reading. They sit outside this project's cryptographic scope and are deliberately framed as limitations warranting scrutiny, not accusations — but an examiner who asks "what else did you notice?" deserves a real answer.

Secondary observations (raised as limitations, not accusations)
  • The ledger is described three different ways. Table 3 says Hyperledger Fabric; §3.6 says the smart contracts ran on a local Hyperledger Sawtooth validator; the same section also describes an adapted permissioned DAG-based ledger with 500 ms block confirmation. These are three different systems with different performance characteristics, so it is unclear which produced the reported latencies.
  • The node count is inconsistent. §3.6 describes a 15-node network; Table 3 and every result specify 50, 100 and 200 nodes (and Table 12 goes to 300). A reader cannot tell which configuration produced which figure.
  • The device specification conflicts with itself. §3.6 says Cortex-M4F with 256 kB flash and 64 kB SRAM under Contiki-NG; Table 3 says Cortex-M4 at 120 MHz with 256 KB RAM and 512 KB flash under RIOT OS. Different operating system, different memory, in the same paper.
  • The comparison table includes a broken scheme without noting it. Table 13 compares PQShield-IoT favourably against "SIKE (NIST) optimized" as a quantum-resilient framework — but SIKE was classically broken in 2022 (Castryck–Decru) and dropped by NIST. A comparison table needs currency checks.
None of these invalidates the framework's design. Together they mean the evaluation needs independent corroboration — which is exactly what this project provides.

§ 4Phase 1 — an environment that works

Every number in this report was produced by real cryptographic code executing on this machine — so before anything could be measured, that code had to install and run. For post-quantum cryptography on a plain Windows laptop, that turned out to be less straightforward than one pip install. The obvious route failed in an instructive way, and the replacement turned out to be arguably the better scientific choice, not a compromise. This section explains both halves, because the credibility of every later number rests on them.

The plan, and why it failed

The original plan was liboqs-python — the Python wrapper around liboqs, the Open Quantum Safe project's library of post-quantum algorithms, written in the C programming language. pip install liboqs-python succeeds — but the package is only a thin shell. The first time you import oqs, it silently downloads the liboqs source code and tries to compile it on the spot, which requires a C compiler and the CMake build tool.

An audit of this machine found none of the required tooling: no cl (Microsoft's C compiler), no gcc (the standard open-source compiler), no Visual Studio Build Tools, no CMake, no WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux), no conda. Installing Visual Studio Build Tools would have meant a multi-gigabyte download requiring administrator rights — a heavy, fragile dependency for a project whose entire point is careful, reproducible measurement.

In plain EnglishThe standard toolkit ships as flat-pack furniture: the box is free, but assembling it needs a workshop full of power tools this machine simply does not have. The fix was to find a supplier that ships the same furniture pre-assembled — and, crucially, furniture from the very same workshop.

The fix — and why it is arguably better

The project instead uses pqcrypto 0.4.0, which ships prebuilt Windows wheels (including for Python 3.14) and binds PQClean — a community project maintaining clean, audited, portable reference implementations of the NIST post-quantum algorithms. This is not a downgrade, and being able to say precisely why matters:

  1. Same code lineage. PQClean is the upstream source that liboqs itself imports for these algorithms. The project did not switch to a different implementation of the cryptography — only to a different packaging of the same one.
  2. Closer to the devices this project is about. PQClean's "clean" implementations are portable C with no AVX2 assembly — much closer to what microcontroller firmware actually runs than a vector-optimised desktop build would be.
  3. Decisively: the embedded benchmark speaks the same code. The pqm4 project (§ 8) compiles these same PQClean implementations for the ARM Cortex-M4. Desktop and embedded numbers in this report therefore describe one codebase measured on two CPUs — the cleanest cross-platform comparison possible without owning the hardware.
AnalogyOne recipe, two kitchens. PQClean is the recipe book; this project cooks from it in a desktop kitchen, while pqm4 cooks the very same recipes on a camping stove. Because the recipes never change, any difference between the two sets of timings measures the kitchens — the hardware — not differences in the cooking instructions. Had we benchmarked a different, desktop-optimised recipe book instead, that clean comparison would have been impossible.

The honest caveat

Honest caveat — stated in the reportAn AVX2-optimised liboqs build would be several times faster in absolute terms than the portable C measured here. Conclusions therefore rest on relative comparisons — scheme against scheme on identical footing — never on absolute desktop speed records. For anyone who wants the optimised route, SETUP.md documents three ways to reproduce the work with liboqs (WSL, Visual Studio Build Tools, conda).

Final stack: Windows 11 · Python 3.14.3 · pqcrypto 0.4.0 (PQClean) · cryptography 49.0.0 (OpenSSL-backed, supplying the classical baseline) · matplotlib · pandas.

§ 5Phase 2 — real benchmarks (Gaps 2 & 3 · benchmark_pqc.py)

The base paper's Table 6 gives four latency numbers with no methodology behind them (Gap 2), and it commits to one signature scheme without comparing the alternatives (Gap 3). Phase 2 answers both by measurement: sixteen schemes benchmarked on one machine under one carefully engineered procedure. Every headline timing in this section is a median in milliseconds, and every choice behind those medians is written down and defensible.

In plain EnglishWe raced the old, quantum-vulnerable algorithms against the new quantum-safe ones on the same computer, timing each operation over and over with laboratory-grade care. The result is a surprise: the new cryptography is essentially as fast as the old. What it really costs is size — its keys and signatures are ten to a hundred times bigger, and for tiny radio-connected devices, size is the expensive part.

First principles — the two kinds of tool being measured

Everything in this phase measures one of two cryptographic building blocks, so it is worth being exact about what each one is. Both belong to public-key cryptography — the branch of encryption that lets two machines that have never met establish trust while the whole world listens in.

AnalogyPublic-key cryptography is a padlock business. Anyone can pick up your open padlock (the public key) and snap it shut on a box — that takes no secret knowledge. But once it clicks shut, only you, holding the one key that fits (the secret key), can open it. Handing out open padlocks by the thousand is perfectly safe, because a padlock reveals nothing about the shape of its key.

A KEM — Key Encapsulation Mechanism — is how two parties agree on a shared secret across an insecure network. It has exactly three operations, and the whole exchange runs like this:

  1. Key generation (receiver). The device that wants to receive secrets runs keygen(), producing a matched pair: a public key, which it may publish freely, and a secret key, which never leaves the device. The public key is the open padlock; the secret key is the only key that opens it.
  2. Encapsulation (sender). The other party runs encapsulate(public key). This single call does two things at once: it invents a fresh shared secret, and it wraps that secret into a ciphertext that only the secret-key holder can unwrap.
  3. The ciphertext travels. Note the asymmetry: only a ciphertext crosses the network — not a second public key. An eavesdropper sees only scrambled data it cannot use.
  4. Decapsulation (receiver). The receiver runs decapsulate(secret key, ciphertext) and recovers exactly the shared secret the sender invented.
  5. Hand-off. Both sides now hold the same secret, which becomes the key for a fast symmetric cipher — here AES-256-GCM — that protects the actual data. A KEM never encrypts user data itself; it only establishes the key. (This KEM-plus-symmetric pattern is called hybrid encryption — a confusingly overloaded word, unrelated to the hybrid key exchange of § 6.)

A digital signature scheme is the mirror image. It also has three operations — keygen(), then sign(secret key, message) → signature, then verify(public key, message, signature) → true/false — but the roles flip: the secret key creates, the public key checks. It is a signet ring pressed into wax: only the ring's owner can make the impression, yet anyone can recognise it. Signatures prove identity and integrity rather than hide content, and they are what the base paper uses Dilithium2 for — device registration and firmware-update authentication.

In plain EnglishA KEM is how two computers that have never met agree on a secret number while everyone is listening; that number then keys the fast conventional encryption that carries the data. A signature scheme is how a computer proves a message really came from it, unaltered. The benchmark times the new quantum-safe versions of both against the classics they must replace.

What was benchmarked — and the fairness rule

The classical baseline — five schemes that are all quantum-broken, included purely as the reference: RSA-2048 (OAEP padding for key transport, PSS for signatures), ECDH P-256 and X25519 for key agreement, ECDSA P-256 and Ed25519 for signatures — the elliptic-curve workhorses of today's internet.

The post-quantum side: ML-KEM-512/768/1024, the standardised lattice KEM at three security levels; HQC-128, the code-based backup KEM (built on error-correcting codes — a different mathematical foundation, so a lattice breakthrough would not take it down too); and three signature families — ML-DSA-44/65, Falcon-512/1024, and SPHINCS+-SHA2-128f/128s, which is built only from hash functions, the most conservative security assumption available.

One design decision matters more than any other for fairness: ECDH and X25519 are benchmarked as KEMs. Their "encapsulation" includes generating an ephemeral keypair, serialising its public key (that serialisation is the ciphertext), validating the received point, and hashing the result through a KDF. Those steps are included deliberately, because ML-KEM's timed C call includes its equivalents. Leaving them out would quietly flatter the classical side.

In plain EnglishTiming two couriers fairly means clocking both door-to-door. ML-KEM's timed operation includes its packing and paperwork, so the classical schemes are timed with their packing and paperwork too — otherwise the old guard would look faster than it really is, and the comparison would be quietly rigged in its favour.

Getting the measurement right

This is the part an examiner is most likely to probe, and it is Gap 2 answered in miniature: not just numbers, but everything needed to trust — or attack — them. Several of these rules were forced by mistakes that had to be found and fixed in review (§ 9); a measurement bug does not crash, it just produces confident wrong numbers.

  • time.perf_counter_ns() — a monotonic high-resolution clock. Never time.time(), which NTP can move mid-run.
  • Pinned to one P-core, high priority. The i5-13500H is a hybrid chip mixing fast P-cores with efficient E-cores — different CPU cores with different speeds. An unpinned benchmark migrates between them and produces meaningless two-humped data. Before pinning, Falcon-512 signing measured 16 ms; pinned, 4.0 ms.
  • Time-based warm-up (≥ 0.25 s, not a fixed call count) so the CPU spools up from its power-saving idle speed to its working frequency before timing starts — even for microsecond-scale operations.
  • Batched sampling for sub-millisecond operations. A 30 µs operation would finish 200 samples inside a single scheduler quantum, so what you would actually measure is "whatever state the CPU was in for those 6 ms". Operations under 1 ms are therefore timed in batches sized so each recorded sample spans ≥ 10 ms of work, and the sample is the batch mean. Slower operations are timed per call, preserving genuine variance — RSA's prime search and ML-DSA's retries are supposed to vary.
  • Garbage collection disabled in the timed region. Python's garbage collector must never land a pause inside a sample.
  • Median as the headline statistic. Operating-system noise is one-sided: preemption and interrupts only ever add time, never subtract it. The median resists that; the mean gets dragged. (The benchmark still records median, mean, standard deviation, minimum and maximum for every operation, so nothing is hidden.)
  • Correctness preflight. Before any timing, every KEM must round-trip its shared secret and every signature must verify. This is not pedantry: ML-KEM's implicit rejection returns wrong bytes rather than raising an error, so a broken benchmark would otherwise run happily, timing garbage.
  • Calibration rows. The harness measures its own overhead — an empty Python call and os.urandom(32) — and records both alongside the results.
In plain EnglishImagine timing a runner three hundred times while a gremlin occasionally leans on the stopwatch — the gremlin can only ever add time, never remove it. The average of all the readings drifts upward with every prod; the middle reading barely moves. That is why the median leads. The other rules are all versions of the same discipline: keep the runner on one track (core pinning), let them warm up first, never time a sprint shorter than the stopwatch's own reaction (batching), and check the runner actually crossed the line (correctness preflight).
