AnalogyAn IoT radio sends postcards, not parcels. IEEE 802.15.4 — the low-power radio underneath Zigbee and Thread — moves at most 127 bytes per frame, roughly 100 of them usable. X25519's 32-byte key is a short note on one postcard. An ML-DSA-44 signature is a 2,420-byte letter that must be cut into about 25 postcard-sized pieces, each mailed separately, each losable, each costing battery to transmit — and one lost piece means asking for it again.
In plain EnglishRead the two result tables together and the story is lopsided. In speed, the quantum-safe newcomers sit right beside the classics — the race is a tie. In size, nothing classical prepares you for them: the standard quantum-safe key-exchange key is 800 bytes where the old one was 32. For a device that pays battery for every byte it radios, that is the whole bill.

What the numbers mean

ML-KEM-512 encapsulation (0.154 ms) matches optimised-assembly ECDH P-256 (0.143 ms) while running unoptimised portable C. A complete post-quantum key establishment costs ~0.4 ms of CPU. What is not free is size: 800 B keys where X25519 uses 32 B.

Pause on how strange that tie is. The classical side runs hand-tuned assembly inside OpenSSL, polished for two decades; the post-quantum side runs plain portable C with no such advantage — and keeps pace anyway. On CPU-class hardware, quantum resistance is essentially free in time. The cost has moved: it now lives in bandwidth.

This reframes the base paper. PQShield-IoT's optimisation layer is built around saving computation — algorithmic pruning, hardware acceleration. Our measurements say that at its own device class, computation was not the binding constraint; bandwidth was. (§ 8 shows where computation does become binding — on microcontrollers, and only for signing-heavy schemes.) Other results worth being able to defend:

  • The three signature families are not interchangeable. ML-DSA signs fast but writes 2,420-byte signatures. Falcon signs slowly — its arithmetic leans on floating-point Gaussian sampling — and its key generation is expensive, yet it has the fastest post-quantum verification measured — of everything benchmarked, only quantum-broken RSA's verify is quicker — with the smallest post-quantum signature. SPHINCS+-128s takes over a second per signature even on this desktop, with 7,856-byte signatures (17,088 B for the fast -128f variant), but rests only on hash functions. Choosing by role rather than habit is the point of Gap 3, and § 8 turns this into a device-class matrix.
  • ML-DSA's signing time genuinely varies — by design, not noise. The algorithm is "Fiat–Shamir with aborts": it drafts a candidate signature, checks whether publishing that candidate would leak information about the secret key, and if so shreds it and tries again, looping until a safe one appears. The number of attempts is unpredictable, so the cost is intrinsically variable. Remember this — it is the key to § 8's sharpest finding.
  • RSA key generation is a randomised prime search with a heavy tail (median 62.2 ms, maximum 235 ms): the algorithm keeps drawing huge random numbers until two turn out to be prime, and luck decides how long that takes. A strong argument that IoT devices should never generate RSA keys on-device.
  • Falcon's signature is variable-length. Its compressed encoding makes the size a distribution, not a constant: ~655 B typical, 752 B PQClean buffer maximum, 666 B in the specification's fixed padded format. The benchmark samples 100 signatures and reports the distribution; an earlier draft quoted one observed length as though exact, and that was itself a review finding (§ 9).
  • HQC-128 is the price of the hedge. The code-based backup runs tens of times slower than ML-KEM at the same security level (Fig 1) and its objects are larger still — 2,249 B keys, 4,433 B ciphertexts. That cost is exactly why HQC is standardised as a backup rather than a default: insurance premiums are supposed to cost something.
In plain EnglishThe quantum-safe algorithms keep up with the classics on a laptop-class processor, so speed is no longer the argument. The argument is luggage: their keys and signatures are enormous, and for battery-powered devices whispering over tiny radios, luggage is what costs. The base paper spent its optimisation effort on speed; the measurements say the real bill was size.

One anomaly, honestly handled

A credible measurement section must also point at the place where its own data is wrong. There is exactly one such place, and diagnosing it teaches more than a clean table would.

Known measurement artefact

Our data shows ML-KEM decapsulation running faster than encapsulation. Every published cycle-count dataset shows the opposite — and must, because decapsulation does strictly more work: it decrypts, then re-encrypts the result to check it (the implicit-rejection design examined in § 7). So our ordering is an artefact; the question is why.

Diagnosis: the encapsulation-minus-decapsulation gap is 90 / 112 / 75 µs across ML-KEM-512/768/1024 — the same order of magnitude throughout, not scaling with the algorithm's cost (on an idle machine it is nearly constant at ~49/46/43 µs). An offset that stays put while the underlying work grows is the signature of a fixed additive overhead — and the operations that carry it (keygen, encapsulation, signing) are exactly the randomised ones, which draw fresh randomness inside the C library on every call.

Two honest qualifications, both surfaced by adversarial review (§ 9). First, the os.urandom calibration row measures 0.20 µs, so it does not quantify a ~92 µs overhead: the magnitude is inferred from the not-scaling-with-work pattern, not measured. Second, for sub-millisecond ordering questions this project therefore defers to pqm4's cycle counts rather than its own wall-clock numbers. Owning a wrong number — and knowing exactly why it is wrong — beats clean data in a viva.

In plain EnglishOne of our stopwatch readings contradicts every published result: we clocked the harder step as faster than the easier one. Detective work shows a small fixed tax lands on certain operations — the ones that pause to gather randomness — and that tax is large enough to flip the order of two already-tiny timings. Rather than hide the oddity, the report explains it, admits which part is inference rather than measurement, and points to a more trustworthy source for that specific question.

§ 6Phase 3 — the hybrid handshake (Gap 1 · hybrid_handshake.py)

A real TCP client and server performing a one-round-trip key exchange in three modes — pure X25519, pure ML-KEM, and hybrid (the deployed TLS 1.3 X25519MLKEM768 construction) — with exact bytes-on-wire accounting and an AES-256-GCM key-confirmation round.

Why hedge at all — the idea of hybrid

A handshake is the opening exchange in which two machines that have never met agree on a shared secret. It follows a protocol: a script both sides know in advance. The question Phase 3 answers is which mathematics the handshake should rest on — and the honest answer, in 2026, is two kinds at once.

A hybrid key exchange derives the session key from two independent exchanges — one classical, one post-quantum — so that breaking either one alone is not enough. That is exactly what TLS 1.3's deployed X25519MLKEM768 group does, and it defends both directions of risk at once:

  • If lattice mathematics turns out to be breakable — the SIKE scenario, where a NIST finalist that had survived years of scrutiny was broken classically in 2022, essentially overnight — the X25519 leg still protects you.
  • If a quantum computer arrives, X25519 falls to Shor's algorithm but the ML-KEM leg still protects you — which is what defeats harvest-now-decrypt-later.
AnalogyFit one door with two different locks — one a time-tested classical design, one a brand-new quantum-proof design — and require both to be picked before the door opens. A burglar who defeats the old lock still faces the new one; a burglar with a clever trick against the new lock still faces the old one. Hybrid key exchange is that door: the session key yields only to someone who breaks both X25519 and ML-KEM. This section prices the second lock — it turns out to cost 64 bytes and a fraction of a millisecond.

The base paper never asks what this insurance costs (Gap 1), which makes the trade-off impossible to weigh. Phase 3 exists to replace that opinion-shaped hole with a measurement. One design note: the classical leg is X25519 rather than P-256 because it is what deployed hybrid TLS actually uses, it was the fastest classical option in Phase 2's data, and its 32-byte public keys keep the hybrid overhead minimal.

In plain EnglishNobody knows which of two disasters comes first: quantum computers breaking today's mathematics, or a clever mathematician breaking the new post-quantum mathematics. A hybrid handshake refuses to bet — it mixes both kinds into one key, so the attacker has to win twice. The world's browsers already do this. The base paper does not, and never says what doing so would cost. This phase measures it.

The protocol, message by message

The implementation is a real client and server talking over a genuine TCP socket, mirroring the one-round-trip shape of TLS 1.3's key_share. Four messages cross the wire:

msg1  client → server : mode ‖ level ‖ [X25519 pub 32 B] ‖ [ML-KEM pub 800/1184 B]
msg2  server → client : [X25519 pub 32 B] ‖ [ML-KEM ciphertext 768/1088 B]

      transcript = SHA3-256(msg1 ‖ msg2)
      K = SHA3-256("CNS-hybrid-v1" ‖ mode ‖ level ‖ ss_x25519 ‖ ss_mlkem ‖ transcript)

msg3  client → server : AES-256-GCM_K(transcript), AAD "c-fin"     } key
msg4  server → client : AES-256-GCM_K(transcript), AAD "s-fin"     } confirmation
  1. Message 1 — the client posts its open padlocks. The client invents two brand-new key pairs for this conversation alone — one X25519, one ML-KEM — and sends the public half of each: a 32-byte X25519 public key plus an 800-byte (level 512) or 1,184-byte (level 768) ML-KEM public key, prefixed by two header bytes announcing the mode (classical, post-quantum or hybrid) and security level it wants.
  2. Message 2 — the server answers with a key and a sealed package. The server sends its own fresh 32-byte X25519 public key — and here is the KEM twist: it does not send an ML-KEM public key back. Instead it runs encapsulation against the client's ML-KEM key, which yields a fresh shared secret (kept) and a ciphertext of 768 or 1,088 bytes (sent). The client opens it with its private key and recovers the identical secret. This asymmetry — both sides contribute a public key on the classical leg, but only a ciphertext returns on the KEM leg — is the shift from classical Diffie–Hellman-style exchange to the KEM style in one picture, and it is what makes a single round trip possible.
  3. Message 3 — the client proves it has the key. Before anything else crosses the wire, both sides privately do the same arithmetic: they feed every byte of messages 1 and 2 through SHA3-256, a hash function, to get the transcript; then they hash a fixed label, the mode and level bytes, both shared secrets and the transcript together to derive the 256-bit session key K. The client now proves it holds K: it encrypts the transcript under K with AES-256-GCM, tagged with the associated data c-fin, and sends the result.
  4. Message 4 — the server proves it back. The server decrypts and verifies the client's proof, then sends its own the same way under the tag s-fin. Only when both proofs verify is the key considered confirmed. If any earlier byte was altered in transit, the two transcripts differ, therefore the two keys differ, therefore GCM authentication fails — and the handshake aborts rather than limping on.

Both legs are ephemeral — a fresh X25519 pair and a fresh ML-KEM pair per handshake — which is what gives forward secrecy. The contrast with the base paper is direct (Gap 6): PQShield-IoT encapsulates against a pre-computed, long-term KEM key, so a single leaked device key retroactively opens every recorded session — precisely the harvest-now-decrypt-later scenario its own introduction warns about. This handshake demonstrates the fix rather than asserting it.

Implementation details that keep the numbers honest
  • TCP_NODELAY is set. Nagle's algorithm — a kernel habit of holding small packets back to batch them into bigger ones — would otherwise dominate the timings; we would be measuring the kernel's batching timer, not cryptography.
  • Frames are length-prefixed. TCP delivers a byte stream with no message boundaries, so every frame carries a 4-byte length prefix and the receiver loops (_recv_exact) until exactly that many bytes arrive. Reported byte counts include the prefixes — they are real wire bytes, not idealised ones.
  • The clock starts before client key generation. Making the ephemeral keys is part of every session's work — that is what ephemeral means — so it belongs inside the timed window.
  • A fresh TCP connection per handshake models session establishment, the thing being priced; the TCP connection setup itself sits outside the timed window either way.
  • The same script demos live: --server and --client run it across two terminals or two machines (--host); by default it self-hosts the server in a background thread so a single command reproduces everything.
In plain EnglishExactly four messages. First, each side hands the other its freshly minted open padlocks (messages 1 and 2). Then each side does the same private arithmetic and arrives at one shared secret number. Finally each sends a sealed note that the other can open only if it computed the very same number (messages 3 and 4). If both notes open, the two sides know — without the key itself ever travelling — that they share a key and that nobody tampered with anything along the way.

Transcript binding and key confirmation

Transcript binding means the KDF consumes a fingerprint of every handshake byte, so the session key depends not only on the secrets but on everything publicly said. Three payoffs follow. First, tampering fails closed: any modified byte anywhere changes the transcript, hence the key, hence the finished messages — the handshake dies loudly instead of proceeding on a corrupted foundation. Second, it satisfies the robustness condition that Giacon–Heuer–Poettering (2018) proved a concatenation combiner needs: the transcript binds both ciphertexts into the key. Third, it defeats downgrade attempts: the mode byte lives inside both the transcript and the KDF label, so an attacker flipping hybrid to classical in flight makes the two sides derive different keys, and the confirmation round exposes it. The same instinct appears in TLS (its key schedule is transcript-bound) and even in the base paper itself, which binds device identities and timestamps into its session key.

Key confirmation — messages 3 and 4 — is each side demonstrating, by successfully encrypting the transcript under the derived key, that it computed the same key over the same conversation. Without it, a key mismatch would only surface later, as garbage in the first real data packet; with it, the handshake itself certifies success or fails on the spot.

Why the construction is secure — stated correctly

The combiner argumentModelling SHA3-256 as a random oracle (equivalently, a secure PRF), the derived key is indistinguishable from random while at least one of the two shared secrets is unknown — so an attacker must recover both. In plain terms: even an adversary who has completely broken one leg and holds that shared secret in full learns nothing usable, because without the other ingredient the hash output still looks like a freshly rolled random number — there is no partial progress, no "warmer or colder". The one-sentence form: under the random-oracle model, the hybrid is at least as strong as the stronger of its two components. The wrong version of this claim — "preimage resistance means you need both secrets" — is not a valid reduction, and an early draft of this project used it before review caught it (§ 9): a function can be perfectly preimage-resistant and still leak whether its output correlates with a known partial input. The KDF also consumes the transcript hash, binding both ciphertexts — the exact condition Giacon–Heuer–Poettering (2018) showed a concatenation combiner needs to be robust — and making tampering fail closed.
AnalogyPicture a machine that takes two secret recipes and prints a paint colour. A weak guarantee would be: nobody can work backwards from the colour to the recipes — that is preimage resistance. But it is not enough: the printed colour could still drift visibly towards red whenever the first recipe is heavy on red, letting an observer learn something without ever inverting the machine. The guarantee the proof actually needs is stronger — the printed colour must look like a colour drawn at random, carrying no trace of either recipe, unless you know both recipes in full. That stronger property is what modelling SHA3-256 as a random oracle provides: withhold either one of the two shared secrets and the derived key is indistinguishable from a random 256-bit string.

Preimage resistance is, however, the right notion for a different question — whether quantum computers threaten SHA3-256 itself. There the answer is reassuring: Grover's algorithm gives at most a quadratic speedup on preimage search, so SHA3-256 retains roughly 128-bit post-quantum preimage resistance — comfortably adequate, and the same assumption the base paper makes for its own SHA3 key derivation.

What this deliberately is not

This is an unauthenticated, ephemeral key exchange — a demonstration of key establishment, not a full authenticated key exchange. Neither side proves who it is, which means a man-in-the-middle can sit inside it. In lay terms: you receive an open padlock in the post claiming to come from your bank, but nothing about the padlock proves it. A corrupt postal clerk can swap in their own padlock — you seal your letter with the clerk's lock believing it is the bank's, the clerk opens it, reads it, re-seals it with the bank's genuine lock and sends it onward. Both ends see a flawless handshake; neither notices the extra party.

Authentication is a separate, deliberately out-of-scope layer: certificates in TLS; blockchain-registered Dilithium identities in the base paper — whose price is exactly what Phase 2's signature benchmarks measure. Naming this boundary before the examiner does is the difference between a limitation and a flaw.

Eight security properties — proven, not asserted

Claims about the key schedule are cheap; executed checks are not. test_handshake_security.py turns each claim into an assertion against the real code, and all eight pass:

  1. Identical keys on honest runs — when nobody interferes, both sides genuinely derive the same key. The protocol works.
  2. The finished message verifies — the key-confirmation round accepts under that shared key.
  3. A tampered transcript yields a different key — change any handshake byte and the two sides' keys silently diverge.
  4. The finished check fails closed on tampering — it raises an error rather than quietly passing; a broken handshake dies, it never limps onward.
  5. Changing the classical secret changes the key — the X25519 leg genuinely feeds the result; it is not decorative.
  6. Changing the post-quantum secret changes the key — the ML-KEM leg genuinely feeds the result too.
  7. Knowing only the post-quantum secret is insufficient — the hybrid property itself: one ingredient alone does not reconstruct the key.
  8. A mode downgrade is detected — flipping the mode byte changes the key, so the finished messages fail authentication; the downgrade is caught, not accepted.
In plain EnglishInstead of writing "our handshake is tamper-proof" and hoping, the project wrote a second program whose only job is to attack the first one — feeding it altered messages, swapped secrets and downgrade tricks — and to verify that every attack visibly fails. All eight attacks fail exactly as the theory says they must.

Results

Each of the five configurations ran 100 handshakes over localhost, reporting the median latency and exact bytes in each direction:

Report table 4 — handshake latency and bytes-on-wire, 100 reps each, localhost TCP (results/handshake_results.csv)
Modemedian msclient→server Bserver→client Btotal B
classical (X25519 only)1.056102100202
pure ML-KEM-5121.3948708361,706
pure ML-KEM-7681.6421,2541,1562,410
hybrid-512 (X25519+ML-KEM-512)2.0769028681,770
hybrid-768 = TLS X25519MLKEM7682.2561,2861,1882,474

Three things to read out of the table. First, the latency ordering — classical, then pure post-quantum, then hybrid — tracks Phase 2's primitive benchmarks, and hybrid costs roughly the classical and post-quantum work summed: nothing mysterious hides in the protocol layer. Second, every configuration completes in about one to two milliseconds — from 1.056 ms for classical to 2.256 ms for hybrid-768 — so on this hardware the compute cost is simply not the story. Third, the sizes are: the classical handshake fits in 202 bytes total, while hybrid-768 needs 2,474 bytes — the same size asymmetry Phase 2 found in the primitives, now visible in a running protocol.

AnalogyAn 802.15.4 radio frame carries about 100 usable bytes — a postcard. The classical handshake is two postcards' worth of conversation. The hybrid-768 handshake is a parcel that the radio layer must cut into roughly 25 postcards, each individually addressed, transmitted, and acknowledged — and if one goes missing, resent. Nothing about the mathematics got slower; the cost moved into the mail room. That is Phase 2's "size, not speed" finding made physical.

Two conclusions follow. First, hybrid over pure post-quantum costs +64 bytes and about +0.6 ms — the 64 bytes being one 32-byte X25519 public key in each direction (an early draft said "+32 B" by counting only one direction; review caught it, § 9). Insurance against a lattice break is nearly free. Second, going post-quantum at all costs about 2.2 kB on the wire — invisible between two processes on a laptop, but roughly 25 radio fragments on a constrained sensor network, where each fragment costs airtime, battery and a chance of loss. The bottleneck for post-quantum IoT is the radio, not the arithmetic.

FindingDefence-in-depth is nearly free. The base paper's pure-PQC choice is something that now needs justifying, not assuming.

§ 7Phase 4 — timing side-channels (Gap 4 · timing_analysis.py)

One idea drives this entire phase: timing is a side channel whenever execution time depends on secret data. An algorithm can be mathematically flawless — unbreakable on paper — and still surrender its key through how long it takes to run. The base paper never asks whether its cryptography leaks this way (that is Gap 4). This phase asks it twice: once on a leak anyone can watch happen, and once on the exact code path that ML-KEM's security stands on.

AnalogyA safecracker does not force the door. She turns the dial slowly and listens for clicks — tiny mechanical tells that say a wheel just seated correctly. The lock's mathematics are sound; the sound gives it away. Timing attacks are the digital version of that. The attacker cannot see the secret, so he listens to the clock instead: code that takes even slightly longer when a guess is slightly more correct is a lock that clicks. Every experiment in this phase is either building a stethoscope or proving a particular door has nothing to hear.

The constant-time rule — and its one exception

The defence against timing leakage is constant-time code: runtime may depend on public things (like input length) but never on secret values, and never on whether a secret check passed or failed. Which operations does the rule cover? Every operation that processes secret material — which turns out to be most of them:

  • Key generation — it samples and manipulates the secret key. Falcon's Gaussian sampling over an NTRU trapdoor is the classic example of a keygen step that must be constant-time.
  • Encapsulation — it generates the random message and the shared secret, so a leak here hands the attacker the session key without ever touching the long-term key.
  • Decapsulation — it uses the secret key directly.
  • Signing — it also uses the secret key.
  • MAC tag comparison — it compares a received value against a secret one.

The notable exception is signature verification, which consumes only public inputs — the public key, the message, the signature. There is no secret in the room, so there is nothing for its variable timing to betray. That exception is the one worth volunteering unprompted in a viva, and it is precisely why Experiment B below targets decapsulation rather than verification: decapsulation is the operation where secret material and attacker-supplied input meet.

On the record: an earlier draft of this project said only decapsulation, signing and tag comparison must be constant-time — omitting keygen and encapsulation. That was wrong, and adversarial review caught it (§ 9). The corrected rule above is the whole rule.

In plain EnglishCryptographic code must take the same amount of time whether your guess was nearly right or completely wrong — otherwise the clock itself becomes a hint machine. This applies to every step that touches a secret. The one step that legitimately may run at variable speed is checking a signature, because everything it looks at is already public.

Experiment A — a leak you can watch happen

The setup is a miniature of a real server. It has computed the correct 32-byte MAC tag for a message, and it compares whatever tag the client sends against it, rejecting mismatches. We measure how long rejection takes as a function of how many leading bytes the attacker already has right — for three different comparison functions doing the same job.

Report table 5 — Experiment A: 32-byte tag comparison, rejection time vs correct prefix (results/timing_analysis.csv)
ComparisonΔ ns (31 − 0 correct)Pearson rVerdict
naive Python loop+2,081+1.000LEAKS (time rises with prefix)
bytes == (memcmp)+18+0.600no exploitable trend
hmac.compare_digest+1+0.832no exploitable trend

The verdict weighs the trend's magnitude against a Welch-z significance gate, not r alone — a flat-but-noisy comparison can show a high r over a sub-nanosecond Δ, which is not an exploitable leak (the naive loop's Δ is three orders of magnitude larger).

The naive early-exit loop — compare byte 0, bail out on the first mismatch — produces a perfect rising staircase: Pearson r = +1.000, with each additional correct byte costing ~67 nanoseconds more, because the loop runs exactly one more iteration before bailing out. That staircase is the attack — the clicks the safecracker was listening for, plotted on an axis:

  1. Send 256 forged tags that differ only in byte 0 — one for each possible value — and time each rejection. The guess that made the server take longest is the one that survived the first comparison: byte 0 is now known.
  2. Fix byte 0 and repeat for byte 1: another 256 timed guesses, keep the slowest. Each round converts a timing difference into one confirmed byte.
  3. March down all 32 bytes. Total work: 256 guesses × 32 bytes = 8,192 attempts — an eyeblink for a script.

Compare that with honest guessing. Without the timing hint, every byte must be right simultaneously, so the attacker faces 2256 possibilities — a number 78 digits long, far beyond what all the computers on Earth could ever enumerate. The leak collapses an impossible search into an afternoon's, because it lets the attacker confirm the tag one byte at a time instead of all at once. That collapse — from multiplying the options to merely adding them — is what every early-exit comparison silently offers.

The fix, hmac.compare_digest, is flat by construction: it accumulates the difference across the whole buffer and only checks the accumulator at the end, so its time depends on length alone. Use it for every secret comparison, always.

The middle row is the subtle one. Python's bytes == calls C's memcmp, which early-exits too — so in principle it leaks the same way. The data mildly agrees: a weak positive trend of r ≈ 0.60 over a spread of only ~18 ns. But that spread is buried under the ~50–100 ns of per-call noise added by Python's interpreter dispatch, so the leak is not exploitable at the Python level. The honest three-part conclusion: the leak exists in principle, it is not measurable through this harness, and it is exactly why C servers must use CRYPTO_memcmp rather than memcmp for secret tags. (The two flat rows sit in the noise, so their exact Δ and r wobble run to run — compare_digest's r can even read high while its Δ stays under a nanosecond. That is why the verdict weighs the trend's magnitude against a Welch z significance gate rather than trusting r alone.)

Why "too small to matter" is never a defenceCould an attacker really exploit a difference of a few hundred nanoseconds across a jittery network? Network noise is thousands of times larger — but attackers average: repeat the same query millions of times and the noise cancels while the signal stays, which is exactly how the Lucky-13 and KyberSlash attacks pulled tiny timing signals out of real systems. The only safe posture is code that is constant-time by construction, not code whose leak is currently inconvenient to measure.
In plain EnglishWe built a door with three different locks and timed how fast each one said "no". The careless lock says no a little more slowly the closer your guess is — so a burglar can find the combination one digit at a time, turning an impossible number of guesses into about eight thousand. The careful lock takes the same time no matter what, so timing tells the burglar nothing. The middle lock (C's memcmp) has the careless design but its tell is drowned out by background noise here — which is a reason to distrust it, not to trust it.

Experiment B — the security-critical post-quantum path

Experiment A demonstrated a leak on purpose. Experiment B checks the path where a leak would be catastrophic: ML-KEM decapsulation. ML-KEM is a KEM, and its claim to the strong IND-CCA2 security level rests on the Fujisaki–Okamoto transform with implicit rejection. On decapsulation the receiver decrypts the incoming ciphertext, then re-encrypts the recovered message and compares the result against the ciphertext it actually received. A genuine ciphertext passes this check; a forged or tampered one fails. And on failure the receiver does not return an error — it silently returns a pseudorandom value derived from a secret, so the caller cannot tell acceptance from rejection.

AnalogyThink of a receptionist checking badges at a secure building. A careless receptionist frowns at fake badges, checks them twice, calls a supervisor — every forged badge teaches the con artist something about what a real badge looks like. The implicit-rejection receptionist is unreadable: real badge or fake, she takes exactly the same time, wears exactly the same expression, and hands over a room key either way — except that the key given for a fake badge opens nothing, and the visitor can never work out whether the badge failed or the key is simply not working. An attacker who probes her with a thousand forged badges leaves with a thousand useless keys and no information.

A detail worth stating precisely, because an earlier draft got it wrong (§ 9): explicit rejection — returning an error symbol instead of a pseudorandom value — is not insecure; both variants are provably IND-CCA2. ML-KEM chose implicit rejection because it admits tighter security proofs in the quantum random-oracle model and because it removes a secret-dependent branch that is genuinely hard to implement in constant time.

The catch that motivates this experiment: if the valid path and the rejection path take different amounts of time, the timing difference itself becomes the oracle the transform was built to deny, and chosen-ciphertext attacks unravel the KEM. This is not hypothetical: the KyberSlash attacks (2023–24) recovered Kyber secret keys because reference decapsulation performed a division whose timing depended on secret data. PQClean and the reference implementation were patched — and this experiment tests the patched code rather than taking the patch on faith.

We timed ML-KEM-512 decapsulation over three interleaved ciphertext classes — valid, one bit flipped, and completely random bytes — and asked whether the classes differ:

Report table 6 — Experiment B: ML-KEM-512 decapsulation by ciphertext class, Δ vs valid (results/timing_analysis.csv)
class (vs valid)Δ medianrelativezverdict
1 bit flipped+25 ns+0.03%-1.5constant-time
random bytes+5 ns+0.01%-0.3constant-time

All three classes overlap within ±1σ, with |z| ≤ 1.5: no oracle detectable at this resolution. The valid path and the rejection path are, to the limits of this measurement, the same length of time — the receptionist really is unreadable. This is the expected result for PQClean's patched implementation; the point of the experiment is that it is now confirmed rather than assumed.

In plain EnglishML-KEM's safety depends on the receiver giving absolutely nothing away when handed a forged ciphertext — not an error message, and not even a different response time. A famous 2023 attack (KyberSlash) broke early implementations exactly this way. We fed the current library genuine, subtly corrupted, and garbage ciphertexts and timed each: all three take the same time to within a few billionths of a second. The door has no clicks that we can hear.

Three measurement traps — the methodology is the contribution

Here is the part that makes this phase more than a demo: the first version of this experiment produced wrong verdicts. Not vague ones — confidently wrong ones, in both directions. Three separate traps had to be engineered out, and each is a general lesson in measurement, not a crypto detail:

  1. A z-test alone over-claims. With n = 300 samples, |z| > 3 flags differences of a few nanoseconds — real in the statistically significant sense, but orders of magnitude below anything exploitable. The first run "found" compare_digest — constant-time by construction — leaking at z = 37. With enough measurements you can prove two coins differ in weight by a speck of dust; that does not make one of them counterfeit. The fix: Experiment A's verdict now rests on the monotonic trend (Pearson r weighted by its magnitude) — because the rising staircase is the attack — with z demoted to a secondary gate.
  2. Sequential measurement lets drift impersonate signal. The first version measured all of class 1, then all of class 2, then class 3. But a CPU is not a fixed instrument: it warms up, shifts frequency, and accumulates state over a run, so when a class was measured confounds what was measured. The fix: classes are now interleaved round-robin — one batch of each class per round — so drift spreads evenly across all three. And this is not merely asserted: the flawed design is preserved as a runnable control. python timing_analysis.py --sequential re-runs the broken protocol (writing results/timing_analysis_sequential.csv) and manufactures a phantom "oracle risk" verdict every time — in the current control run a +0.18% phantom difference reported significant at z = +4.7, and in an earlier recorded control as extreme as a −55% difference at z = −18.9 — from pure CPU-state drift, on the identical operation the interleaved design reads as constant-time at |z| ≤ 1.5. The phantom's magnitude and even its sign change run to run, which is itself the tell: a real leak would be stable; drift is not.
  3. Reusing one input inflates z. A single fixed input per class makes the within-class variance artificially tiny — so any per-object artefact, such as one buffer happening to sit favourably in the CPU's cache, reads as hugely significant. The fix: each class cycles through a pool of 16 fresh inputs, so no single object's quirks can drive the statistics.
The lessonA naive measurement design invents a leak that is not there — and, crucially, collecting more samples would not have helped: it would only have estimated the biased value more precisely. Removing a systematic confound requires changing the design, not the sample size. The sequential control makes this contrast reproducible on demand, which is the single best evidence in the project that measurement design matters.
The statistics, defined (no scipy required)

Batch-mean samples. As in the Phase 2 benchmark, each sample times a batch of calls and divides by the batch size, lifting sub-microsecond operations safely above the timer's granularity.

Welch z = (mean₁ − mean₂) / √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂): a two-sample difference test that does not assume the two groups have equal variances. With n in the hundreds it behaves like a standard normal under the null hypothesis, so |z| > 3 means roughly 99.7% confidence that a difference exists — not that the difference is exploitable, which is exactly why Experiment A adds the trend gate.

Pearson r: the correlation of median rejection time with prefix length — the exploitability measure for the tag-comparison leak, because the attack works precisely when time rises monotonically with correctness.

In plain EnglishOur first attempt at this experiment accused innocent code and could have acquitted guilty code — because the measuring process itself was biased. Three fixes: stop treating "statistically detectable" as "actually dangerous"; alternate between the things being compared instead of testing them one after another (so the machine warming up cannot masquerade as a leak); and vary the test inputs so one atypical input cannot skew the result. We deliberately kept the broken version as a switch you can flip, and it fabricates a leak on demand — the clearest possible proof that how you measure decides what you find.

What is honestly not claimed

This method resolves only leaks that are large relative to desktop timing noise — hundreds of nanoseconds. Experiment A's tag-comparison leak is comfortably above that floor, which is why it shows up as a textbook staircase. KyberSlash was not: it was a few-cycle division-timing leak, far below what black-box wall-clock timing on a busy laptop can resolve. And since Experiment B runs only against already-patched constant-time code, there is no positive control at that scale — no known-leaky few-cycle specimen against which to prove the harness could detect one.

Not claimedThis project does not claim its method would have caught KyberSlash. Detecting few-cycle leaks needs instruction-level tooling in the style of dudect — statistical timing tests driven millions of times at cycle resolution against deliberately leaky controls — which is listed as future work (§ 11). Stating the resolution floor plainly is what keeps Experiment B's "no oracle detected" an honest, bounded claim rather than an overreach.

§ 8Phase 5 — from desktop to device (Gap 5 · pqm4_extrapolation.py)

The obvious objection to everything measured so far — "you benchmarked a laptop; IoT devices are not laptops" — is correct, and this phase answers it. The bridge is pqm4, the community-standard benchmark of post-quantum cryptography on the ARM Cortex-M4, whose published cycle counts come from real STM32 silicon compiled from the same PQClean source this project benchmarks: one codebase, two CPUs. Cycle counts are the exact (clock-independent) metric; pqm4's milliseconds are quoted at its 24 MHz convention. Falcon-512 carries an asterisk, explained beneath the table.

Why a laptop can say anything about a microcontroller

First, be clear about how different the two machines are. A microcontroller like the ARM Cortex-M4 is a complete computer on one chip: it executes one simple instruction at a time, in order, with kilobytes of memory and no operating system to speak of. The laptop processor measured in § 5 (an Intel i5-13500H) runs near 4.6 GHz across multiple CPU cores, keeps megabytes of cache close to the arithmetic, and uses instruction-level parallelism to execute several instructions per tick. These are not two sizes of the same thing; they are different classes of machine.

The honest way to compare across them is the clock cycle. A processor's clock speed, quoted in MHz, says how fast the metronome ticks; the cycle count says how many ticks a piece of code needs, which is a property of the code and the processor design, not of the frequency it happens to be run at. That is why pqm4 publishes cycle counts as its primary result, and why this project treats cycles as the ground truth and cross-platform milliseconds as merely indicative. pqm4 quotes its millisecond figures at 24 MHz deliberately: at higher clocks the chip's slow flash memory forces the processor to insert flash wait-states, which would contaminate the counts. A real 168 MHz STM32F407 deployment would be roughly 5–7× faster than the 24 MHz figures — but not cleanly so, precisely because of those wait-states.

The legitimacy of the bridge rests on one fact established in § 4: pqm4's "clean" implementations are compiled from the same PQClean C source that the desktop benchmark runs through pqcrypto. This is not a comparison of two libraries that happen to implement the same maths; it is one body of code, measured on two processors — the cleanest cross-platform statement possible without owning the silicon. And crucially, pqm4's numbers come from real hardware, independently measured and publicly published — which is exactly the kind of evidence the base paper's simulator-only methodology lacks.

AnalogyPQClean's source code is a recipe. This project cooked it in a restaurant kitchen (the laptop) and timed every step; pqm4 cooked the identical recipe on a camping stove (a real Cortex-M4) and published exactly how long each step took. One recipe, two kitchens — so any difference in timing is the kitchen, not the recipe. Comparing two different recipes across two kitchens would tell you nothing.

The one asterisk: Falcon-512's clean reference implementation does not fit in pqm4's RAM — Falcon's key generation needs unusually large working memory — so its row uses pqm4's optimised m4-ct build instead, and is flagged as such in the CSV. That a standardised scheme's reference code cannot physically load on the benchmark board is itself a data point for the device matrix below.

In plain EnglishWe do not own the tiny chip, so we borrowed the most trusted public measurements of it — measurements taken on real hardware running the exact same code we timed on the laptop. Because the code is identical, the comparison is apples-to-apples: it isolates what the machine costs, not what a different implementation costs. And instead of comparing raw seconds between a fast machine and a slow one, we count the processor's heartbeats, which is fair to both.

The desktop-to-device gap

Report table 7 — one PQClean codebase, two CPUs (results/pqm4_comparison.csv; pqm4 cycles from real STM32 silicon)
Operationdesktop i5-13500HCortex-M4 @ 24 MHzslowdown
ML-KEM-512 encapsulate0.154 ms29.2 ms~189×
ML-KEM-512 decapsulate0.064 ms37.0 ms~576×
ML-DSA-44 sign0.572 ms330 ms~577×
Falcon-512 verify *0.066 ms10.6 ms~161×
SPHINCS+-128s sign1,189 ms319 s (5.3 min)~268×

* Falcon's clean build does not fit pqm4's RAM; its row uses the optimised m4-ct implementation — that memory-fit fact is itself device-matrix evidence.

The slowdown is plausible on its face: the raw clock ratio alone is ~190× (≈4.6 GHz vs 24 MHz), and the observed spread of roughly 160–580× brackets it — instruction-level parallelism, cache and memory bandwidth account for the variation around the pure clock ratio. Nothing here is mysterious; it is simply what happens when portable C moves from a wide superscalar core with megabytes of cache to a 24 MHz in-order chip.

Here the base paper's framing becomes true. Phase 2's headline was that on CPU-class hardware the cost of post-quantum cryptography is bytes on the wire, not computation. On a Cortex-M4 that partially inverts. ML-KEM stays comfortable — tens of milliseconds per operation, entirely workable for a device that establishes a key occasionally. But ML-DSA signing takes ~330 ms, and SPHINCS+-128s signing takes 319 s — about 5.3 minutes for one signature. Computation re-emerges as a binding constraint as a function of device class — refining Phase 2's conclusion, not contradicting it, and motivating the device matrix that closes this section.

In plain EnglishMoving from a laptop to a sensor-class chip makes everything a few hundred times slower — as expected, since the chip's heartbeat is about 190 times slower and it does less per beat. Key exchange survives the move fine: a few hundredths of a second. Some signatures do not: one takes a third of a second, and the most conservative one takes over five minutes. So "is the maths fast enough for IoT?" has no single answer — it depends on which chip, and which job.

The implied-clock test — the sharpest finding

Now test the base paper's Table 6 — its claimed on-device latencies — against measured silicon. Doing this correctly requires care, because there is a trap, and this project itself fell into it once (§ 9): you must not mix clocks. pqm4 reports milliseconds at its 24 MHz convention; the paper's Table 3 declares its device as an "ARM Cortex-M4 (120 MHz)". Comparing the paper's numbers directly against pqm4's 24 MHz milliseconds manufactures a discrepancy out of a unit difference — an earlier draft of this analysis did exactly that, produced a headline "7.9× optimistic" figure, and adversarial review killed it. Rescale honestly to the paper's own declared 120 MHz and the picture becomes stranger, not simpler:

The clock-mismatch check — the paper's Table 6 vs pqm4 rescaled to the declared 120 MHz
Operationpaperpqm4 @ 120 MHzpaper ÷ pqm4
Kyber512 encapsulate28 ms5.84 ms4.80× (paper slower)
Kyber512 decapsulate31 ms7.41 ms4.19× (paper slower)
Dilithium2 sign42 ms66.05 ms0.64× (paper faster)
Dilithium2 verify36 ms17.19 ms2.09× (paper slower)

At its own declared clock, the paper is pessimistic on three operations and optimistic on one. No single scaling factor reconciles all four — so arguing about which clock to assume is a dead end. Ask the clock-independent question instead: what clock would each Table 6 entry need, in order to be a genuine cycle-accurate measurement? The arithmetic is deliberately simple:

  1. Take pqm4's measured cycle count for an operation — a fact about this code on real silicon (for Kyber512 encapsulation: 700,605 cycles).
  2. Take the paper's claimed latency for the same operation (28 ms).
  3. Divide cycles by time. 700,605 cycles in 28 ms is possible only on a processor ticking at about 25.0 MHz — that operation's implied clock.
  4. Repeat for all four operations, and compare the four implied clocks with the single declared 120 MHz device.
Report table 8 — the implied-clock test: pqm4 measured cycles ÷ the base paper's Table 6 ms = the clock each entry would need (device declared: 120 MHz)
Operationpqm4 cyclespaper's latencyimplied clock
Kyber512 encapsulate700,60528 ms25.0 MHz
Kyber512 decapsulate888,65331 ms28.7 MHz
Dilithium2 sign7,925,95542 ms188.7 MHz
Dilithium2 verify2,063,09636 ms57.3 MHz
Four operations, one declared 120 MHz device — and the four implied clocks span 25 to 189 MHz, a 7.5× spread. No processor runs at four frequencies at once, so Table 6 cannot be cycle-accurate measurement of the declared device, whatever clock is assumed.
AnalogyFour stopwatches each claim to have timed the same runner on the same track, and the runner's stride count is known exactly. Work backwards from each stopwatch's reading and one implies the runner took 25 strides a second, another 29, another 189, another 57. Individually each reading looks fine; together they cannot all describe that runner. The implied-clock test does the same with the paper's four latencies: cycles are the strides, the declared 120 MHz device is the runner, and the four "stopwatches" disagree by 7.5×.

This is the strongest form of the finding precisely because it needs no assumption about the paper's hardware or frequency. It does not say "the paper's numbers disagree with our clock guess"; it says the four numbers are mutually inconsistent — they cannot all be honest timings of any single device at any single clock.

What this does and does not prove. It does not prove fabrication, and this project never says so. The likely explanation is mundane: the latencies came from some unstated mapping — a host-machine measurement, a simulator's timing model, a scaling factor applied unevenly. That is exactly Gap 2 restated with evidence: not "no real library was used" (the paper names PQClean and liboqs), but no measurement methodology was reported, so the numbers cannot be attributed to anything — and now they demonstrably cannot be attributed to the declared device. One suggestive detail: signing — the single operation where the paper is faster than measured silicon — is also the single operation whose cost is data-dependent. ML-DSA signs by Fiat–Shamir with aborts (§ 5): it loops, discarding candidate signatures that would leak information about the secret key, so its true cost includes retries — exactly the component a fixed-cost timing model most naturally under-counts. Offered as a hypothesis, not a conclusion.

In plain EnglishThe paper claims one chip produced four timings. We asked each timing: how fast would the chip's heartbeat have to be for you to be a real measurement? The four answers disagree wildly — from 25 to 189 million beats a second, for a chip declared to run at 120 million. That does not mean anyone lied. It means the numbers came from some shortcut the paper never describes — which is precisely the complaint: it reports timings without ever saying how it measured them.

The RFC 7228 device-class matrix

The final deliverable turns all of the above into deployment guidance. RFC 7228 is the IETF's standard vocabulary for constrained devices, classifying them by memory: Class 0 (≪ 10 KiB RAM, ≪ 100 KiB flash) are motes that cannot run post-quantum cryptography alone and must lean on a gateway; Class 1 (~10 KiB RAM, ~100 KiB flash) are CoAP-class nodes where PQC fits only with care; Class 2 (~50 KiB RAM, ~250 KiB flash) can host a full PQC stack; anything above Class 2 — gateways and edge servers — can run everything, hybrids included. The base paper's simulated node (64 KiB SRAM, 256 KiB flash) sits at the top of Class 2: genuinely constrained, but comfortable for its chosen schemes — the matrix shows what breaks one class down, where its design would actually struggle.

Each verdict below blends three measured costs: pqm4 latency (compute), published peak stack usage (memory), and bytes on the wire from this project's own size data (radio).
