  • ML-KEM-512 is the practical KEM floor: ~3 KB stack and sub-40 ms per operation, so it fits even Class 1 on compute. But its 800 B public key and 768 B ciphertext fragment heavily over 802.15.4's ~100 B payloads. The pinch is the radio, not the CPU — Phase 2's conclusion surviving the trip down to silicon.
  • ML-DSA-44's binding constraint is not time but memory: a ~50+ KB signing stack, which rules out Class 1 entirely yet is comfortable on Class 2 — the paper's node, vindicating that particular choice.
  • Falcon-512 has the best verify-side profile measured anywhere in this project: ~11 ms on an M4 with a ~655 B signature. Key generation (~3 s) and its floating-point-heavy signing belong on a gateway.
  • SPHINCS+ signs in minutes on an M4, so only its verification is deployable on-device. Its reward is conservative, hash-only security — worthwhile exactly when the signing can happen elsewhere.
  • Hybrid X25519+ML-KEM-768 costs +64 B on the wire (+32 B each direction) and sub-millisecond compute over pure ML-KEM: the cheap insurance a Class 2 node should simply take. Below Class 2, offload the handshake to a gateway.

The one-line lesson: match the scheme to the role and the device class. Falcon's ~3 s key generation sounds disqualifying — until you notice that a sensor verifying firmware updates only ever runs Falcon verify (~11 ms, tiny signature). Key generation and signing happen once, on the vendor's gateway; the constrained node only ever checks. Judged as "a scheme for IoT", Falcon looks unusable; judged as "the verify half of a firmware-update role", it is the best option measured.

In plain EnglishThink of devices in T-shirt sizes. The smallest (Class 0) cannot do this cryptography at all and need a chaperone. Small (Class 1) can manage key exchange but not the big signature schemes — one of them needs more scratch memory than the whole device owns. Medium (Class 2, the paper's device) handles the standard toolkit comfortably. And the golden rule is to ask not "is this algorithm fast enough for IoT?" but "which job does this device actually do — and does the algorithm's cost for that job fit this size?" A chip that only checks signatures never pays the cost of creating them.

§ 9How the work was quality-controlled

Benchmark code deserves the same scrutiny as the code it measures — and arguably more, because its failure mode is worse. Nothing in this project was accepted merely because a script printed it. Every program, every claim and every quoted figure went through three adversarial review passes, and 54 findings — real bugs and real errors of reasoning — were confirmed and fixed. This section explains how that worked, and honestly catalogues what it caught.

The failure modeBroken application code crashes — you notice. Broken measurement code runs to completion and prints confident, plausible, wrong numbers — you do not notice, and every conclusion built on those numbers inherits the error. That asymmetry is why a project whose entire contribution is measurement must treat its own tooling as a suspect, not a witness.
In plain EnglishThe project deliberately hired its own opposition. Instead of asking reviewers "is this good?", it asked several specialist reviewers to attack the work from different angles — the cryptography, the measurement technique, the arithmetic, the sceptical examiner's point of view. Every accusation those reviewers produced was then handed to three further reviewers whose only job was to prove the accusation wrong. Only accusations that survived that counter-attack were accepted as genuine problems — and every single one that survived was fixed, not explained away.

Adversarial review with refute-voting

Each pass examined the work through multiple reviewer lenses: cryptographic correctness (is the security reasoning actually valid?), measurement methodology (do the numbers measure what they claim to?), numeric consistency (does every figure agree with every other copy of itself?), and a strict-examiner perspective (which sentence would a hostile viva examiner attack first?). The lenses generate candidate findings — but candidate findings are cheap, and a false accusation is costly in the opposite direction: fixing a non-problem wastes effort and buries real signal.

Hence the second stage, refute-voting: every candidate finding was put to three independent reviewers with the explicit instruction to refute it — to find the reason the accusation is mistaken. Only findings surviving a majority vote were treated as real. The scepticism is symmetric: the process distrusts the work and distrusts criticism of the work, and only what survives both directions of attack is acted on.

AnalogyImagine submitting an article to a panel of hostile editors, each expert in a different way articles go wrong — one checks the logic, one the arithmetic, one the sourcing, one reads it as your harshest critic would. But any accusation an editor raises is then passed to three colleagues told: your job is to prove this accusation false. Accusations that collapse under that counter-attack are discarded; the ones that survive are treated as facts and the article is corrected. An accusation that has survived a determined attempt to kill it is worth far more than one that was merely voiced.
3
independent adversarial review passes
54
confirmed findings — 22 + 20 + 12 across the three passes
3
refute-voters per candidate finding — majority vote to survive
54/54
findings fixed — none waived or excused

The three passes moved outward from the code: 22 findings in a first pass over the benchmark itself, 20 in a second over Phases 3–5 plus the report and the literature survey, and 12 in a third over the project's explanatory documentation — and that third pass is where the two most serious errors in the whole project were caught: the overstated Gap 2 critique of the base paper, and the clock-mismatch in the headline finding (both detailed below). The lesson generalises: prose that describes results can be just as wrong as code that produces them, and it deserves the same hostility.

Bugs found in the measurement code

In plain EnglishFive genuine bugs lived in the measurement tooling. None of them crashed anything — each one quietly produced wrong or misleading numbers, which is exactly the failure mode the warning box above describes. Each bullet ends with why it mattered.
  • --quick silently did nothing. Python evaluates a function's default arguments once, at definition time, so def bench(fn, budget_s=TIME_BUDGET_S) froze the full-run value; reassigning the global later had no effect. Worse, the environment record then claimed quick parameters while full ones were actually used. Fixed by reading configuration at call time.
    Why it matters — a tool that misreports its own settings poisons the provenance of every number it produces: you can no longer say which configuration generated which result.
  • Core pinning failed silently. Pinning locks the benchmark to a single CPU core so it cannot wander mid-measurement. The Windows call GetCurrentProcess() returns the pseudo-handle −1; without explicit ctypes HANDLE type declarations that value was truncated to 32 bits, and both Win32 system calls quietly failed, returning False. It was caught only because the pinning status string was recorded and printed rather than assumed.
    Why it matters — every timing in the project depends on pinning; a silent failure means meaningless data with no crash to warn you. Always check the return value of a best-effort system call.
  • Unpinned timing was meaningless anyway. The i5-13500H is hybrid P-core/E-core silicon: an unpinned benchmark migrates between fast and slow cores mid-run. Falcon-512 signing measured 16 milliseconds unpinned versus 4.0 ms pinned.
    Why it matters — that is a 4× error — larger than most of the differences the project's conclusions rest on. Left in place, it would have swamped every real finding.
  • Fixed-count sampling measured the scheduler, not the cryptography. An operation taking ~30 µs finishes hundreds of samples inside a single scheduler time slice — so what you record is whatever state the CPU happened to be in for those few milliseconds, not the algorithm's cost. Replaced with batched sampling: fast operations are timed in batches sized so each sample spans at least 10 ms.
    Why it matters — it was timing the machine's mood, not the mathematics. The median of a biased sample is still biased.
  • Duplicate keygen rows disagreed with each other. RSA key generation was measured twice, minutes apart, and reported 38 ms in one table and 280 ms in another — both "correct", because the machine warmed up between them. Fixed: measure once, report the same row everywhere.
    Why it matters — two different numbers for one fact in one document is an instant credibility loss; and machine warm-up is a real effect that must be controlled, not averaged over.

Errors found in the claims

In plain EnglishThe code was not the only place mistakes lived. The sentences — the security arguments, the criticisms of the base paper, the quoted figures — were reviewed with the same hostility, and nine of them turned out to be wrong or unsupportable. Several of these corrections made the project's findings stronger, not weaker.
  • The hybrid combiner's justification was cryptographically wrong. The combiner is the function that merges the classical and post-quantum secrets into one session key. An early draft argued its security from "preimage resistance" of the hash function — but a function can be perfectly preimage-resistant and still leak correlations. The correct notion is random-oracle/PRF indistinguishability. Corrected in every document.
    Why it matters — the construction was right and the reasoning was wrong; in cryptography a correct thing believed for the wrong reason is a time bomb, because the wrong reason will eventually justify a wrong thing.
  • An unsupported number. The report claimed a "~46 µs RNG overhead quantified via calibration" — but the calibration actually measures os.urandom at 0.13 µs, some 350× smaller. Reworded as an explicitly inferred quantity, deferring to pqm4's cycle counts for sub-millisecond ordering questions.
    Why it matters — claiming a guess was a measurement is precisely the sin this project accuses the base paper of. The distinction between measured and inferred is the project's whole currency.
  • A clock-mismatch error in the old headline finding. The base paper's Table 6 was compared against pqm4 milliseconds computed at 24 MHz while the paper declares a 120 MHz device — manufacturing a dramatic "7.9× optimistic" discrepancy out of a unit mismatch. Replaced with the clock-independent implied-clock test of § 8, which is both correct and stronger.
    Why it matters — the project nearly committed the exact class of error it critiques. The corrected analysis needs no assumption about the paper's hardware at all — which is why it is unanswerable.
  • An overstated critique of the base paper. An early draft claimed the paper "used no real cryptographic library". False: the paper's §3.6 explicitly names PQClean and liboqs, and an examiner can find that sentence in seconds. Narrowed to the defensible and still decisive gap: no measurement methodology is reported, so the numbers cannot be attributed to anything.
    Why it matters — one falsifiable overstatement destroys the credibility of every accurate criticism around it. Critique must be precise or it is worthless.
  • Falcon's signature was treated as a constant. Falcon uses a compressed encoding, so its signature length genuinely varies from one signature to the next (~655 bytes typical, 752 maximum). Quoting one observed length as exact — and checking it for equality — was wrong. The benchmark now samples 100 signatures and records mean/min/max, documents quote a range, and the verifier range-checks that row.
    Why it matters — treating a distribution as a constant makes automated checks fail randomly and quietly teaches readers a false fact.
  • Inconsistent figures across documents. The hybrid handshake's overhead appeared as +32 B in some files and +64 B in others — 64 is correct: one 32-byte X25519 public key travels in each direction. ML-KEM-512's public key appeared as 768 B — that is its ciphertext size; the public key is 800 B.
    Why it matters — cross-document drift is how honest projects end up contradicting themselves in front of an examiner; it is the exact disease the verifier (below) was built to cure.
  • An unreproducible claim. The report cited a "z = 3.4 false positive" from an early timing run whose data had been lost. Rather than softening the wording, a --sequential control mode was added to the timing experiment so the flawed-measurement effect regenerates on demand — and it proved far more dramatic than the lost original: an earlier recorded control reached z = −18.9, and the current run shows z = +4.7. The magnitude and even the sign flip run to run — itself the tell that it is thermal drift, not a real leak.
    Why it matters — the gold standard response to "citation needed" is not better wording but a button that regenerates the evidence.
  • Two constant-time misstatements. First, an early draft said only decapsulation, signing and tag comparison need constant-time implementations — wrong: key generation and encapsulation also handle secret material and need it too. Second, it said an explicit rejection error "would itself be an oracle" — also wrong: both variants of the Fujisaki–Okamoto transform are provably IND-CCA2; ML-KEM chose implicit rejection for tighter proofs and easier constant-time implementation, not because explicit rejection is insecure.
    Why it matters — a report that teaches cryptography must not teach wrong cryptography, even in passing.
  • An overclaim about detection power. A draft implied the timing methodology "could catch KyberSlash-scale leaks". It could not — that attack lived at few-cycle resolution, far below this harness's noise floor, and there was no positive control to prove otherwise. The claim was removed (see the limitations in § 11).
    Why it matters — a security tool that overstates its own sensitivity gives false assurance, which is worse than giving none.

A case study from the final week: the sizes.csv crash

Quality control is not a phase that ends; it is a net that keeps catching. The most recent catch is instructive enough to tell in full. During the first full benchmark re-run of the current cycle, the run crashed while writing sizes.csv — the CSV file recording every key and signature size.

  1. The seed was planted by an earlier fix. When adversarial review established that Falcon's signature length is variable (above), the fix added two new fields — observed_min_bytes and observed_max_bytes — but only to the variable-length signature rows. From that moment the table's rows were heterogeneous: most rows had one set of columns, the Falcon rows had two extra.
  2. The writer assumed homogeneity. The code handed csv.DictWriter the header sizes[0].keys() — the column names of the first row, a fixed-size row without the extra fields. The moment the first Falcon row arrived carrying keys the header never declared, DictWriter raised ValueError and the run died mid-file.
  3. The bug was latent, then punctual. Nothing was wrong on the day the Falcon fix landed; the crash could only trigger on the next full run that wrote all the rows — which is exactly when it did. A bug can sit harmless in code for weeks, armed by one change and detonated by another.
  4. The net caught the debris. The crash itself was loud, and the half-written sizes.csv it left behind was immediately flagged by the verifier script rather than silently feeding wrong sizes into the report.
  5. The fix respects heterogeneity. The header is now built as the ordered union of keys across all rows, with restval="" filling the blanks in rows that lack a field.
AnalogyImagine printing a survey form by copying the column headings from the first person's answer sheet. Everything works — until someone arrives with an extra answer for which no column exists, and the clerk refuses to continue, abandoning the stack half-processed. The repaired process reads everyone's sheets first and prints a column for every answer that appears anywhere, leaving blanks where a person had nothing to say.

The story earns its place here because it compresses three lessons the whole section teaches: fixes plant bugs (the correction of one review finding created this crash); assumptions about data shape are load-bearing (a table whose rows differ needs a header built from all of them); and guard systems pay for themselves (the failure was caught by machinery, not luck).

The permanent guards: a verifier and a builder

Fifty-four fixes would be worth little if the fifty-fifth error could creep in unnoticed next month. So the review process ends not with a clean bill of health but with two standing guards that run after every benchmark re-run:

  • verify_report_numbers.py — the verifier. Every headline number quoted in the report is listed alongside the CSV it came from, and re-checked against it: sizes and byte counts must match exactly (they are deterministic), timings are allowed a 20% band for laptop drift, and Falcon's signature is range-checked because its length is genuinely variable. It caught the half-written sizes.csv above within seconds of the crash.
  • build_html_report.py — the builder. This very page is not hand-edited: every timing-dependent number and all of its data tables are generated from the CSVs at build time, and the build fails loudly if any placeholder is left unresolved. A page rebuilt from the data cannot drift from the data the way a hand-maintained document can.
In plain EnglishTwo robot proof-readers stand guard permanently. One re-reads every number in the report and checks it against the raw data files; the other rebuilds this entire web page directly from those files, so a stale number cannot survive a rebuild. Humans make the claims once; machines re-check them forever. Quality control here is not an event that happened — it is a property the project keeps.

§ 10Conclusions

Five phases, eight programs, eight datasets and seven figures converge on a single paragraph. It answers the question posed at the start — not "is post-quantum cryptography secure?" but "does it fit on small devices, and what does it cost?" — and the answer relocates the cost to a different place than the base paper assumed.

Post-quantum cryptography is not primarily a computational problem for IoT. On CPU-class hardware, standardised lattice cryptography costs microseconds; the real cost is bytes on the wire — 800-byte keys and 2,420-byte signatures against ~100-byte radio frames. Computation binds only at microcontroller class, and only for signing-heavy schemes. The correct engineering response is role- and device-class-aware scheme selection, plus hybrid key exchange — 64 bytes of insurance against a cryptanalytic break.
In plain EnglishMaking IoT devices safe from future quantum computers does not make them meaningfully slower; it makes their messages bigger. On anything with a real processor, the new quantum-safe mathematics runs as fast as today's — the extra time is measured in millionths of a second. The pain is that its keys and signatures are ten to a hundred times larger, and tiny radio devices send data in postcard-sized packets. The right response is not one heroic algorithm but choosing the right scheme for each job and each size of device — and, for a few extra bytes, running the old lock and the new lock together so both would have to fail.

Reading the thesis, clause by clause

  1. "Not primarily a computational problem." Measured head-to-head on the same pinned core, ML-KEM-512 key exchange encapsulation took 0.154 ms against 0.143 ms for elliptic-curve ECDH P-256 — within 8% — and its decapsulation (0.064 ms) was faster still, even though the post-quantum side ran unoptimised portable C against hand-tuned assembly. A complete quantum-safe key establishment costs about 0.4 ms of CPU. On CPU-class hardware, quantum resistance is essentially free in time.
  2. "The real cost is bytes on the wire." ML-KEM-512 puts an 800-byte public key and a 768-byte ciphertext on the network where X25519 puts 32 bytes each way; ML-DSA-44's signature is 2,420 bytes. The radio underneath Zigbee and Thread, IEEE 802.15.4, carries roughly 100 usable bytes per frame — so one post-quantum key needs about 8 fragments and one signature about 25, and fragmentation costs battery and multiplies loss. On radio networks, bandwidth, not computation, is where post-quantum cryptography hurts.
  3. "Computation binds only at microcontroller class, and only for signing-heavy schemes." Move from a laptop to a microcontroller and the picture partially inverts: at pqm4's 24 MHz Cortex-M4 convention, ML-KEM remains comfortable at tens of milliseconds, but ML-DSA-44 signing takes ~330 ms and SPHINCS+-128s signing takes 319 seconds — over five minutes. Key establishment stays cheap everywhere; it is signing that becomes a binding constraint, and only on the smallest devices. This refines Phase 2 rather than contradicting it.
  4. "Role- and device-class-aware scheme selection." The signature families are not interchangeable, and their weaknesses can be routed around by role. Falcon-512's ~3-second key generation sounds disqualifying — until you notice that a sensor verifying a firmware update only ever runs Falcon verify (~11 ms, ~655-byte signature — the best verification profile measured). The § 8 device-class matrix turns this into a rule: match the scheme to the role and the device class, and let gateways do what motes cannot.
  5. "64 bytes of insurance." A hybrid key exchange costs one extra 32-byte X25519 key in each direction (+64 bytes) and about +0.6 ms over pure ML-KEM-768. Lattice cryptanalysis is young, and SIKE — a NIST candidate that survived years of scrutiny — fell to a classical attack in 2022. Against that history, 64 bytes is not a cost worth debating; it is a premium worth paying.

Against the base paper, point by point

The project set out to extend and verify PQShield-IoT, not to demolish it — and the fairest summary begins with credit. Five conclusions, each self-contained:

  1. Its cryptographic design choices are sound, and its Kyber modelling matches real silicon within ~20%. Kyber512 and Dilithium2 were the right NIST picks for constrained devices; keeping AES-256-GCM and SHA3-256 for the symmetric layer is exactly what the quantum threat model prescribes. And the paper's two Kyber timings are consistent, to within about 20%, with what measured Cortex-M4 cycle counts predict — though at a ~25 MHz effective clock (pqm4's 24 MHz reporting convention), not at the 120 MHz the paper declares (§ 8) — evidence that this part of its simulation was anchored to something real, even if the clock behind it was never stated. Criticism means more when it sits beside earned credit.
  2. Its optimisation layer optimises the resource that was not the binding constraint. PQShield-IoT's optimisation machinery — algorithmic pruning, hardware acceleration — is built to save computation. But at the paper's own declared device class, measurement says computation was already cheap; the scarce resource was bandwidth: 800-byte keys against 100-byte radio frames. In plain terms: the paper installed a faster engine in a car whose actual problem is that the road is too narrow. The effort is not wasted — computation does bind on smaller devices — but the paper optimises the wrong axis for the device it models.
  3. Its Table 6 latencies imply four different processor clocks, so they cannot be cycle-accurate measurements of the declared device. Divide independently measured cycle counts by the paper's four reported latency figures and you get the clock speed each figure would require to be a genuine cycle-accurate measurement: 25.0, 28.7, 188.7 and 57.3 MHz — a 7.5× spread for four operations in one table on one declared device. No processor runs at four frequencies at once, whatever clock you assume. This does not prove fabrication, and the project does not claim it does; the likely explanation is an unstated mapping between some host measurement and the modelled device. But that is precisely the point: when no methodology is reported, the numbers cannot be attributed to anything — and this is the concrete, arithmetic cost of that omission.
  4. Its pure post-quantum design forgoes hybrid protection that measurement prices at 64 bytes. The paper uses Kyber alone: if lattices ever fall the way SIKE fell, every PQShield-IoT session key falls with them. Deployed practice — the default in Chrome, Firefox and Cloudflare's TLS — hedges with a hybrid. The paper never asks what hedging would cost; this project measured it: +64 bytes and well under a millisecond. At that price, the pure-PQC choice is something a designer must justify, not something to assume by default.
  5. It claims forward secrecy while its protocol cannot provide it — and the Phase 3 handshake demonstrates the difference. Forward secrecy requires ephemeral keys; the paper's protocol encapsulates every session against a device's static, long-term KEM key. An attacker who ever obtains that one key can therefore decrypt every recorded past session — and the extra ingredients the paper's key-derivation function stirs in (identities, timestamps) are all public, so they add freshness but no secrecy. This is the very harvest-now-decrypt-later scenario that motivates post-quantum cryptography in the first place. The project's own handshake generates fresh X25519 and fresh ML-KEM keys per connection and destroys them afterwards — so the difference between claiming forward secrecy and providing it is not asserted here; it is demonstrated in running code.

One meta-conclusion sits above all five: a number without a methodology cannot be audited, only believed. Everything this project measured is attributable — to a script, a CSV, a recorded environment, a guard that re-checks it — and the sharpest finding against the base paper (point 3) required nothing more than taking its numbers seriously enough to do arithmetic on them. The strongest compliment the project can pay PQShield-IoT is that its design survives measurement — refined, reframed, but standing; what does not survive is the practice of publishing performance claims with no stated way to check them.

§ 11Limitations & future work

Volunteered before an examiner asks — that reads as competence. A limitations list is not an apology; it is a precise statement of what the evidence does and does not support, which is the difference between a measurement project and a marketing document. Each limitation below states what it is, why it exists, how much it could distort, and — where one exists — the future-work item that would close it.

In plain EnglishEvery study has weak spots. The honest move — and the tactically smart one — is to name yours first, with numbers, before someone else names them for you. None of the seven below undermines the project's conclusions; several, examined closely, actually strengthen them. And five of the seven come with a concrete plan for how the next iteration would fix them.

Seven limitations, stated plainly

  1. Implementation asymmetry. The classical baseline is OpenSSL's hand-tuned assembly; the post-quantum side is PQClean portable C with no AVX2. Classical-versus-PQC gaps are therefore upper bounds on post-quantum cost — an optimised PQC build would only look better. Note that this cuts for the headline conclusion, not against it: ML-KEM matched ECDH despite the handicap. In plain terms: the amateur ran barefoot against a professional in spikes and still kept pace — proper shoes would only widen the story in the amateur's favour.
  2. Laptop measurement. Despite core pinning and high process priority, a consumer laptop shows tens-of-percent variance — and the project measured this effect on itself. The idle overnight run (2026-07-17) recorded ML-KEM-512 encapsulation at 0.084 ms; the current browser-open run records 0.154 ms — ~1.8× for this operation, ~1.6× averaged across all operations, and near-uniform across every algorithm, classical and post-quantum alike, because busy cores drain the shared power and thermal budget and the pinned core clocks down. Crucially, nothing relative moved: every ordering, ratio and conclusion held. Medians, a recorded environment (system_info.txt) and interleaved measurement mitigate the noise; they do not eliminate it. In plain terms: on a crowded running track everyone's times slow together — the finishing order, which is what the conclusions rest on, is preserved.
  3. Cross-platform millisecond figures are indicative, not exact. The desktop-to-microcontroller comparison is exact only in clock cycles, which are clock-independent; the millisecond translations use pqm4's 24 MHz convention, and a faster real device would not scale cleanly because higher clocks stall on slower flash memory. The Cortex-M4 comparison is therefore qualitative: reliable about which schemes are feasible where, not about decimal places.
  4. The timing analysis is black-box. Phase 4 observes execution time from the outside, through Python, so it resolves only leaks that are large against desktop noise — Experiment A's hundreds-of-nanoseconds staircase is comfortably visible, but KyberSlash lived at few-cycle resolution, far below this floor, and the method has no positive control at that scale. Experiment B's verdict is therefore precisely scoped: no oracle detectable at this resolution — not no leak exists. In plain terms: this is a stethoscope, not an MRI — it hears the loud problems and says nothing about the quiet ones.
  5. The handshake is unauthenticated — by design. Phase 3 demonstrates key establishment, not a full AKE, so a man-in-the-middle could sit inside it. Authentication is a separable layer — certificates in TLS, blockchain-registered signing identities in the base paper — and its ingredients were priced separately in Phase 2's signature benchmarks. The scoping is deliberate and stated before an examiner can raise it.
  6. Standardised ≠ the paper's exact schemes. This project benchmarks the FIPS-final ML-KEM and ML-DSA; the paper cites their round-3 ancestors Kyber512 and Dilithium2. Same design lineage, near-identical cost — but not bit-compatible, and the project's own data proves it: ML-DSA-44's secret key is 2,560 bytes (the FIPS 204 size), not round-3's 2,528. Likewise the SPHINCS+ benchmarked is the v3.1 submission, not final SLH-DSA. In plain terms: the final published edition of a cookbook versus its draft — the dishes taste the same, but ingredient lists differ by a line, so components cannot be swapped byte-for-byte.
  7. The blockchain layer was not reimplemented. It lies outside this project's cryptographic scope. The paper's internal inconsistencies there — it describes its ledger three different ways (§ 3) — are noted as observations warranting scrutiny, not investigated as findings. In plain terms: this project audited the locks, not the ledger.

Natural next steps

Each next step is the closure of a limitation above — future work as a plan, not a wish list:

  • An authenticated hybrid handshake — add ML-DSA or Falcon signatures over the handshake transcript and measure the full AKE cost, closing limitation 5. Phase 2 already priced the parts; this assembles and times the whole.
  • First-party measurement on a real Cortex-M4 board — replace extrapolation from pqm4's published counts with cycle counts collected on owned silicon, closing limitation 3 and removing the last inference from the desktop-to-device bridge.
  • Instruction-level constant-time verification — run dudect-style statistical testing and ctgrind-style instrumentation, which provide exactly the few-cycle resolution and the positive control that limitation 4 says the black-box method lacks.
  • Fragmentation-level simulation over a real 6LoWPAN/802.15.4 stack — convert bytes-on-wire into what a battery actually feels: energy per handshake and probability of loss per fragment. This would put hard numbers under the thesis's central claim that bandwidth, not computation, is where post-quantum cryptography bites.
  • An adaptive scheme-selection layer consuming the device-class matrix — the base paper's own "algorithmic pruning" idea, realised with measured data underneath it instead of simulation. It is the constructive ending the project aims at: not replacing PQShield-IoT's vision, but giving it the evidence base it was missing.

The arc of the five is the arc of the project itself: first measure the true cost of post-quantum security, then engineer around the costs that are real — and only those.

§ 12Reproducing everything

A result you cannot re-run is a result you have to take on faith — and this project is built so that nothing has to be taken on faith. Every timing, every table and every figure in this report regenerates from a handful of short commands on any ordinary Windows machine with Python installed. Each script writes its raw results as CSV files; the figures are drawn from those files; and this very page is assembled from them, so the words can never quietly drift away from the data.

In plain EnglishThis section is the recipe card. Install four ready-made ingredients, run seven short programs in order, and you will have rebuilt every number in this report from scratch on your own computer — plus an automatic checker that compares what the report claims against what your machine just measured, and a builder that regenerates this web page itself.

The commands, and what each one produces

Run these from the project folder, in this order. Each line's comment names the gap it closes (§ 3) and roughly how long it takes.

pip install pqcrypto cryptography matplotlib pandas
cd code
python benchmark_pqc.py              # Gaps 2+3  (~3 min; --quick = smoke test, overwrites CSVs)
python hybrid_handshake.py           # Gap 1     (~30 s, 100 reps)
python timing_analysis.py            # Gap 4     (~2 min; --sequential adds the drift control)
python pqm4_extrapolation.py         # Gap 5     (instant — cited pqm4 data)
python plot_results.py               # fig1–fig7
python test_handshake_security.py    # 8 security properties
python verify_report_numbers.py      # report ↔ CSV consistency guard

What each command actually does, one at a time:

  1. pip install … — one-time setup. It fetches the four ready-made libraries the project depends on: pqcrypto (the post-quantum algorithms, prebuilt, binding PQClean), cryptography (the OpenSSL-backed classical baseline), matplotlib (drawing) and pandas (data handling). Nothing to build, no extra tools, no administrator rights.
  2. benchmark_pqc.py — the heart of the project. It benchmarks all 16 schemes, classical and post-quantum, timing every operation thousands of times on a pinned CPU core. In plain terms: it races every lock-and-key design on the same track and writes down the stopwatch readings. It produces results/timings.csv (51 rows — every operation's median, mean, spread and extremes), results/sizes.csv (17 rows of key, ciphertext and signature sizes), and results/system_info.txt — the provenance record of exactly which machine, power plan and library versions produced the run. The --quick flag is a smoke test (~50 s): useful for checking nothing is broken, but be warned that it overwrites the canonical CSVs with low-quality numbers.
  3. hybrid_handshake.py — performs 100 real client–server handshakes per configuration over a genuine network connection on the local machine, in all five modes (classical, pure post-quantum at two strengths, hybrid at two strengths). It writes results/handshake_results.csv: the median latency and the exact number of bytes each side sent, length prefixes included.
  4. timing_analysis.py — stages the two side-channel experiments: the watchable MAC-tag comparison leak, and the check that ML-KEM decapsulation runs in constant time. Adding --sequential deliberately re-runs the experiment with a flawed measurement design, as a control that manufactures a phantom leak from thermal drift — proof that the methodology, not just the sample count, matters. Outputs: results/timing_analysis.csv (27 rows) and, with the flag, results/timing_analysis_sequential.csv.
  5. pqm4_extrapolation.py — instant, because it does no benchmarking of its own. It combines this project's desktop measurements with pqm4's published cycle counts for the Cortex-M4 microcontroller, runs the implied-clock consistency test against the base paper's Table 6, and derives the device-class recommendation matrix. Outputs: results/pqm4_comparison.csv (22 rows) and results/device_class_matrix.csv (9 rows).
  6. plot_results.py — redraws all seven report figures (results/fig1–fig7, PNG) from whatever the CSVs currently contain. If a CSV is missing it skips that figure rather than failing.
  7. test_handshake_security.py — executes the eight security assertions of § 6 in about a second: tampering fails closed, a downgrade is detected, and knowing only one of the two secrets is insufficient. It exits with an error code if any property fails, so it doubles as an automated regression test — and it is the single best thing to run live in a viva.
  8. verify_report_numbers.py — the guard. It re-checks every number quoted in the report against the CSV it came from: sizes and byte counts must match exactly, timings are allowed a laptop-drift band, and Falcon's genuinely variable-length signature is range-checked rather than equality-checked. If a number in the text has silently gone stale, this script says so before an examiner does.

Rebuilding this very page

One more command closes the loop. build_html_report.py regenerates PROJECT_REPORT.html — the page you are reading right now — from a template plus the CSVs and figures:

python build_html_report.py          # regenerates PROJECT_REPORT.html (this page) from the CSVs

Every timing-dependent number and all the data tables in this page are read from the CSVs at build time, and the figures are embedded directly into the file (encoded as base64 text), so the page is one self-contained document that opens in any browser with nothing to install. The builder fails loudly if any placeholder in the template is left unresolved — by design, an incomplete page can never be produced silently. Run it, together with the verifier, after any benchmark re-run.

The two-terminal live demo

python hybrid_handshake.py --server                              # terminal 1
python hybrid_handshake.py --client --mode hybrid --level 768    # terminal 2

Open two terminal windows. The first command starts a server that sits listening; the second launches a client that connects to it, performs the full § 6 hybrid exchange — the same construction TLS 1.3 deploys — and prints the negotiated mode, the measured latency and the exact bytes sent in each direction. Watching two genuinely separate programs agree on a secret key across a real network socket is the most persuasive sixty seconds this project can offer: nothing is mocked, and every byte is counted.

Benchmark hygiene — why the machine must be idle

Benchmark hygieneRun on AC power with the browser closed. Background CPU load makes every timing 1.5–2.5× slower, near-uniformly (the busy cores drain the shared power/thermal budget, so even the pinned benchmark core clocks down) — an effect this project measured on itself, below. Sizes and byte counts are deterministic and unaffected.

Why does a busy laptop slow a benchmark that is pinned to its own core? Because a modern chip cannot run all of its CPU cores flat-out at once: the whole chip shares a single power and heat budget. When background programs — a browser with twenty tabs, a video call, an indexing service — keep the other cores busy, those cores draw from the shared budget, and the benchmark's core must lower its clock speed to keep the chip within its power and temperature limits. Every operation then takes proportionally longer, even though the benchmark core is doing nothing different.

AnalogyThink of the chip as a kitchen stove with one gas line feeding four burners. Light one burner and it roars; light all four and every flame shrinks, because they share the supply. Pinning the benchmark to one burner does not help if the other three are lit — the shared gas line, not the burner, is the limit. Closing the browser turns the other burners off.

The project measured this effect on itself, and the two full runs on record are the evidence. The idle overnight run (2026-07-17) measured ML-KEM-512 encapsulation at 0.084 ms; the current run (2026-07-27, browser and editor open — the run every number in this report traces to) measures 0.154 ms — ~1.8× slower for this operation, ~1.6× averaged across all operations, near-uniformly across everyalgorithm, classical and post-quantum alike, with heavier background load pushing the slowdown towards the upper end of the 1.5–2.5× range the box above quotes. Crucially, because the slowdown is uniform, nothing relative moved: ML-KEM still sits within ~8% of ECDH, hybrid still costs +64 bytes, and the implied-clock finding never depended on local timings at all. Sizes and byte counts are immune entirely — they are counted, not timed, and a byte is a byte however hot the chip runs.

§ 13File map

The project lives in a single repository: a folder tree of documents, code, data and figures, each file existing for exactly one reason. This map is written so that a stranger opening the folder for the first time can navigate it without asking anyone.

In plain EnglishThink of the folder as a well-kept laboratory notebook in four parts: the story documents (what was done and why), the experiments (eight Python programs), the raw data (every measurement and figure), and the formal write-up (the IEEE-format paper and this web page). Everything cross-references everything else, and nothing is left over.

If you are new here, read in this order

  1. README.md — the two-minute overview: what the project claims and how to run it.
  2. PROJECT_REPORT.html — this page: the whole story with figures, tables and definitions inline.
  3. EXPLANATION.md — the same story at full depth, from first principles.
  4. The code/ scripts, each next to its *_EXPLAINED.md deep dive, when you want to see how a specific experiment works.
  5. VIVA.md — the night before the exam.
Everything in the repository and why it exists
PathWhat it is
EXPLANATION.mdThe complete narrative, first principles → conclusions — why quantum computers break today's cryptography, what the base paper does, the six gaps, all five phases with results, the quality control, and what remains open. The authoritative source this page condenses; read it to understand the project.
VIVA.mdThe defence pack: a 60-second pitch, the gap→contribution→evidence table, the numbers to know cold, four concepts to explain on demand, likely examiner questions with answers, and the weaknesses worth volunteering before being asked. Built for revision, not reading.
README.md / SETUP.mdThe front door and the workshop manual. README.md is what a marker sees first: gap table, headline findings, run commands. SETUP.md explains the environment — why pqcrypto was chosen over liboqs, three documented fallback routes, and the benchmarking hygiene rules (AC power, browser closed).
PROJECT_REPORT.htmlThis very page — the self-contained illustrated report with all seven figures embedded and every data table generated from the CSVs. Opens in any browser with nothing to install; the best single file to show someone or present from.
base-paper/…pdfNarayanan et al. (2026) — the PQShield-IoT paper being extended and critiqued. Every section reference in this report (§3.2, §3.6, §4.9, Tables 3 and 6) points into this PDF.
literature-survey/survey.mdThe literature survey, organised as six threads — standardisation, constrained hardware, algorithm diversity, hybrids, side channels, and blockchain+PQC — each ending in the gap it exposes, followed by a synthesis table mapping the threads onto this project's contributions.
code/benchmark_pqc.pyGaps 2+3 — the largest script (~560 lines): the 16-scheme benchmark. Contains the timing engine (time-based warm-up, the garbage collector disabled, batched sampling for sub-millisecond operations), core pinning at high priority, calibration rows that measure the harness's own overhead, and correctness preflights that prove every scheme round-trips before it is timed.
code/hybrid_handshake.pyGap 1 — a real TCP client and server performing the one-round-trip key exchange in three modes (classical, post-quantum, hybrid), then confirming the key with an encrypted "finished" exchange. Measures handshake latency and exact bytes-on-wire, length prefixes included.
code/test_handshake_security.pyTurns the handshake's security claims into demonstrated facts: eight assertions covering fail-closed tampering, the hybrid property (knowing one secret is not enough) and downgrade detection. Exits non-zero on any failure, so it doubles as a regression test.
code/timing_analysis.pyGap 4 — both side-channel experiments: the tag-comparison leak you can watch happen, and the ML-KEM decapsulation oracle test. The --sequential flag re-runs the deliberately flawed measurement design as a control, proving the interleaved methodology matters.
code/pqm4_extrapolation.pyGap 5 — the desktop-to-device bridge: cited pqm4 Cortex-M4 cycle counts (compiled from the same PQClean source), the implied-clock test that exposed the base paper's mutually inconsistent Table 6, and the RFC 7228 device-class matrix. Runs instantly; it benchmarks nothing itself.
code/plot_results.pyDraws all seven figures from the CSVs — dot plots on logarithmic axes (bar lengths lie on a log scale, so dots are used instead), one colour per algorithm family, and a dagger on every quantum-broken scheme so status is never encoded by colour alone.

All timing numbers and data tables are filled in at build time and the figures embedded as base64, so the page cannot drift from the data; it fails loudly if any placeholder is left unresolved.
report/PROJECT_REPORT_template.htmlThe HTML template behind this page: all the prose and styling, with placeholders where the measured numbers and tables go. build_html_report.py fills them from the CSVs — the separation that keeps words and data honest with each other.

results/Every number and figure: 8 CSV/TXT datasets (timings, sizes, handshake results, both timing-analysis runs, the pqm4 comparison, the device matrix) plus the fig1–fig7 PNGs and system_info.txt — the provenance record naming the CPU, power plan, pinning status and library versions behind each benchmark run.
report/report.tex + references.bibThe formal IEEE-format report (IEEEtran two-column style) and its bibliography — NIST standards, RFC 7228, pqm4, KyberSlash, PQClean and the base paper. Written in LaTeX; no LaTeX toolchain is installed locally, so compile it on Overleaf (a free in-browser LaTeX service) — report/README.md has step-by-step instructions and the figure manifest.

Safe to ignore: code/__pycache__/ is Python's automatically created cache of compiled files — not part of the project, and deletable at any time.

§ 14Viva quick answers

The questions most likely to be asked, with the answers this project can back with data. (Full pack: VIVA.md.)

In plain EnglishA viva is a spoken exam where the examiner probes for weak spots. The strongest defence is not memorised answers — it is having measurements, controls and admitted mistakes standing behind every claim. Each question below opens to show exactly that. Click any question to expand it.

Challenges to the work

"Your results are on a laptop. Why should I believe anything about IoT?"
Two answers. First, laptop numbers are never claimed to be IoT numbers — they are extended with pqm4's published Cortex-M4 cycle counts, compiled from the same PQClean source this benchmark runs: one codebase, two CPUs. Second, the base paper has no hardware measurement at all; measured-plus-cited beats simulated. Put simply: rather than pretending a laptop is a sensor, the project measures the code once and lets the embedded community's published measurements of the same code speak for the small device.
"Optimised assembly vs portable C — isn't your baseline unfair?"
It is asymmetric, and it is stated as a limitation — but it is conservative for the conclusion: the handicap makes PQC look worse, and ML-KEM matches ECDH anyway. What is not claimed: precise classical-vs-PQC ratios. Those are upper bounds on PQC cost. In everyday terms, the race was run with the post-quantum side carrying a backpack — hand-tuned assembly against plain portable C — and it kept pace regardless.
"Why is your decapsulation faster than encapsulation?"
Measurement artefact, not physics — decapsulation does strictly more work (the FO re-encryption check). The randomised operations carry a fixed ~92 µs overhead inside the C library, shown by the encaps−decaps gap staying near-constant while the algorithm scales. The os.urandom calibration (0.20 µs) does not quantify it, so it is inferred, not measured — and for ordering questions the project defers to pqm4 cycle counts. The plain-English version: the stopwatch also captures the time the randomised operations spend gathering fresh randomness inside the library, which pads encapsulation but not decapsulation.
"How do you know your timing analysis isn't noise?"
Because the control is built in: --sequential reproduces the flawed design and manufactures a phantom oracle verdict (z = +4.7 in the current control run; an earlier recorded control reached |z| ≈ 19) from CPU-state drift, on the same operation the interleaved design reads as clean. Interleaving removes a systematic confound that more samples would only estimate more precisely. In plain terms: if you time all of A while the machine is cold and all of B after it has warmed up, B looks slower even when they are identical — alternating A and B round-robin is the cure, and the phantom's changing size and even sign between runs (its z-score) is exactly how you know it was drift, not a leak.
"Would you have caught KyberSlash?"
No, and the report says so. KyberSlash was a few-cycle division leak; the resolution floor here is hundreds of nanoseconds, and there is no positive control at that scale. That requires dudect-style instruction-level tooling. A few CPU ticks is like a microsecond gap in a hand-timed race — below anything this stopwatch can resolve, and claiming otherwise would be exactly the kind of overclaim the review process removed.
"Falcon keygen takes seconds. Why recommend it for IoT?"
Role matters more than scheme. A sensor verifying firmware only ever runs Falcon verify — ~11 ms on an M4 with a ~655 B signature, the best verify-side profile measured. Keygen and signing happen once, on the vendor's gateway. That is what the RFC 7228 matrix encodes. It is the difference between printing a passport — slow, done once, at an office — and glancing at one at the border, fast and done constantly.
"Is your handshake secure?"
As a key exchange, yes — eight properties proven by test (tamper fails closed, downgrade detected, knowing only the PQ secret is insufficient). But it is deliberately unauthenticated — an ephemeral exchange, not an AKE (authenticated key exchange); a MITM can sit in it. Authentication is the signature layer's job, and Phase 2 prices it. Think of two strangers building a perfectly private tunnel: the tunnel itself is sound, but nothing yet proves who stands at the far end — that proof is a separate, and separately priced, layer.
"What's wrong with the base paper?"
Avoid "wrong". The design is reasonable. Two substantive issues: (1) evaluation methodology — latencies with no host, timing method, repetitions or variance, whose four values imply mutually incompatible clocks (25–189 MHz); (2) forward secrecy claimed with static long-term KEM keys, which does not provide it. Secondary: ledger described three ways, node counts vary, SIKE listed as quantum-resilient after its 2022 break — raised as limitations to investigate. The forward-secrecy point in one line: the paper locks every conversation against the same long-term key, so one future theft of that key opens every recorded conversation at once.
"Doesn't the paper say it used real PQC libraries?"
Yes — §3.6 names PQClean and liboqs, and this project says so. The critique is not "no library"; it is "no measurement methodology reported, so the numbers cannot be attributed". And since the paper used PQClean — the same source pqm4 compiles — the cycle-count comparison is same-codebase, which makes it harder to dismiss. In short: the complaint is not "fake ingredients" but "no recipe card" — nobody can tell how the reported timings were produced, on what hardware, or scaled how.
"What did you get wrong, and how do you know?"
Plenty, on record (§ 9): a --quick flag that silently did nothing (default-argument binding), core pinning that failed silently (ctypes HANDLE truncation), 16 ms→4 ms Falcon once pinned, a security argument corrected from preimage-resistance to PRF indistinguishability, and a clock-mismatch error in an earlier headline finding — replaced by the implied-clock test. Three adversarial review passes, 54 confirmed findings, all fixed, and a verifier script so numbers can't silently drift again. The lesson carried forward: measurement code fails silently rather than crashing, so every claim in this report now has an automated check standing behind it.

Concept checks

"Why pqcrypto and not liboqs?"
Necessity first: liboqs-python compiles the liboqs C library from source on first import, and this machine has no compiler, no CMake, and no administrator rights for the multi-gigabyte Build Tools download. pqcrypto ships prebuilt Windows packages and binds PQClean — which is the upstream source liboqs itself imports for these algorithms, so it is the same code lineage. Arguably it is the better choice: PQClean's portable C, with no AVX2 assembly, is closer to what microcontroller firmware actually runs, and pqm4 compiles those same implementations for the Cortex-M4 — making Phase 5 a one-codebase, two-CPU comparison. The honest caveat, stated in the report: an AVX2-optimised liboqs build would be several times faster in absolute terms, so conclusions rest on relative comparisons, and SETUP.md documents three routes to reproduce with liboqs if desired. In plain terms: the substitute ingredient turned out to come from the same farm as the original — and to match the target device's diet more closely.
"What exactly is a KEM, and how is it different from Diffie–Hellman key exchange?"
A KEM never encrypts user data. The sender encapsulates against the receiver's public key, producing a ciphertext plus a shared secret; the receiver decapsulates the ciphertext with its secret key and recovers the same secret; the data then travels under AES-256-GCM. The structural difference from classical Diffie–Hellman: in DH both sides send public keys and combine them symmetrically; in a KEM only a ciphertext comes back — that asymmetry is the whole DH-to-KEM shift the post-quantum migration forces. The padlock version: the receiver publishes an open padlock (the public key); the sender snaps it shut around a freshly generated secret and posts the locked box (the ciphertext) back; only the receiver's private key opens it. Both sides now hold the same secret, and nothing secret ever travelled unprotected.
"If quantum computers break RSA and ECC completely, why does AES-256 survive?"
Because the two known quantum attacks are wildly unequal. Shor's algorithm breaks the mathematics under public-key cryptography — factoring and discrete logarithms — in polynomial time, so no bigger key can save RSA or elliptic curves. Grover's algorithm, the only quantum lever against a symmetric cipher, gives only a quadratic speedup: it effectively halves the key length. AES-128 falls to ~64 bits of security — too weak — but AES-256 retains ~128 bits, which remains comfortably strong, and Grover parallelises poorly, so real machines do worse than the theory. Hence the design rule this whole field follows, base paper and project alike: replace the public-key parts, keep the symmetric parts with big keys — which is exactly why both keep AES-256-GCM for bulk encryption and SHA3-256 for key derivation. One-line version: quantum computers pick the locks on the front gate, not the vault door — so the migration replaces the gate and keeps the vault.

§ 15Glossary

Every technical term this report leans on, alphabetised and defined for a reader with no cryptography background. Dotted-underlined words throughout the page show these definitions on hover or keyboard focus; this table is the permanent reference, so the page never has to be left to be understood.

In plain EnglishIf a word anywhere above made you pause, it is in this table — plain meaning first, precision second.
A–Z of terms
AEADAuthenticated encryption with associated data — encryption that both scrambles the data and produces a tamper-evident integrity tag, and can additionally authenticate unencrypted metadata travelling alongside. AES-GCM provides both confidentiality and integrity in one construction.
AES-256-GCMThe workhorse symmetric cipher used for the encrypted session in both the base paper and this project's handshake. Its 256-bit key keeps it strong even against Grover's quantum search — the reason the symmetric layer survives the quantum transition unchanged.
AKEAuthenticated key exchange — key establishment plus identity proof, so each side also knows who it just agreed a key with. This project's handshake deliberately is not one: it builds the private tunnel but does not check passports.
AlgorithmA precise, step-by-step recipe a computer follows to solve a problem. Every cipher, signature scheme and benchmark in this report is an algorithm; the cryptographic ones are recipes easy to run forward and believed impossible to run backward without the key.
BandwidthHow much data a communication link can carry per unit of time. IoT radios have very little of it — an 802.15.4 frame carries only ~100 usable bytes — which is why the size of post-quantum keys, not their speed, turns out to be the real cost on CPU-class hardware.
BenchmarkA controlled experiment that runs an operation many times under carefully fixed conditions to measure how fast it truly is. The measured alternative to simulating or guessing — and the core of Phase 2.
ByteEight bits; the basic unit of digital size, roughly one character of text. An X25519 public key is 32 bytes; an ML-DSA-44 signature is 2,420 — the gap that drives this report's thesis.
CiphertextThe scrambled, unreadable output of encryption. In a KEM the word also names the sealed package the sender transmits — the locked box carrying the material from which both sides derive their shared secret.
Clock speed / cycleA processor's heartbeat: one cycle is a single tick of its internal clock, and clock speed (MHz or GHz) counts ticks per second. Cycle counts are the clock-independent way to compare an algorithm across machines — the foundation of § 8's implied-clock test.
CombinerThe recipe that merges the classical and post-quantum shared secrets into one session key — in this project, feeding both (concatenated, with the transcript hash) into the SHA3-256 key-derivation function. A sound combiner guarantees the key stays safe while either ingredient remains secret.
Constant-timeRuntime independent of secret values, so an attacker with a stopwatch learns nothing. Required for keygen, encapsulation, decapsulation, signing and tag comparison — not for signature verification, which handles public inputs only.
Digital signatureThe public-key counterpart of a handwritten signature: the signer's private key produces a stamp over a message that anyone can check with the public key, proving who sent it and that nothing changed in transit. ML-DSA, Falcon and SPHINCS+ are the post-quantum options compared here.
Encapsulate / decapsulateThe two travelling operations of a KEM. The sender encapsulates against the receiver's public key, producing a ciphertext plus a shared secret; the receiver decapsulates the ciphertext with its secret key to recover the same secret.
EncryptionTransforming readable data into unreadable ciphertext with a key, so only holders of the right key can reverse it. The mathematical lock on essentially all private digital communication.
Entropy / randomnessUnpredictability. Cryptographic keys must be drawn from high-quality randomness (the operating system's os.urandom here), because a predictable key is a guessable key. Gathering randomness also takes time — the likely source of § 5's encapsulation-timing artefact.
Fiat–Shamir with abortsML-DSA's signing loop: it repeatedly generates candidate signatures and discards any that would leak information about the secret key, keeping the first safe one. This retrying is why signing time varies from message to message.
FIPS 203 / 204 / 205The three post-quantum standards NIST published in August 2024: ML-KEM (key establishment, formerly Kyber), ML-DSA (signatures, formerly Dilithium) and SLH-DSA (hash-based signatures, formerly SPHINCS+).
FO transformFujisaki–Okamoto: the construction that turns a weaker (IND-CPA) encryption scheme into a strong (IND-CCA2) KEM via a re-encryption check plus implicit rejection — decrypt, re-encrypt, and confirm the result matches what arrived.
Forward secrecyThe guarantee that compromising long-term keys today must not expose sessions recorded in the past. It requires ephemeral per-session keys that are destroyed after use — which is precisely what the base paper's static KEM keys fail to provide.
Harvest-now-decrypt-laterRecording encrypted traffic today, cheaply, to decrypt it the day quantum capability arrives. The reason "we'll upgrade when quantum computers exist" fails for any data with a long confidentiality lifetime. Defeated by forward secrecy plus post-quantum key exchange.
Hash functionA one-way blender: any input in, a fixed-size fingerprint out. Easy to compute, practically impossible to reverse or to find two inputs sharing a fingerprint. SHA3-256 derives the session keys throughout this project.
Hybrid key exchangeDeriving the session key from both a classical and a post-quantum exchange, so breaking one alone is insufficient — two locks on one door, needing both picks. Distinct from hybrid encryption, which merely means public-key crypto establishing a symmetric key.
Implicit rejectionOn a decapsulation mismatch, return a secret-derived pseudorandom value instead of an error message. This removes a secret-dependent branch that is hard to make constant-time and tightens the security proofs in the quantum random-oracle model.
IND-CCA2The strong security notion a KEM should meet: it stays safe even against an attacker allowed to submit chosen ciphertexts and observe the decapsulation results — the adversarial setting real networks provide for free.
IoTInternet of Things — everyday objects (sensors, meters, industrial controllers) fitted with small computers and radios. The hard case for post-quantum cryptography: tiny compute, tiny memory, tiny radio frames, and 10–20-year deployments that die with the cryptography they shipped with.
KEMKey encapsulation mechanism: keygen / encapsulate (→ ciphertext + shared secret) / decapsulate. It establishes a symmetric key between two parties; it never encrypts user data itself — the data then travels under AES-GCM.
KeyThe secret ingredient that makes a cipher lock or unlock. Symmetric ciphers use one shared key, like two copies of a house key; public-key systems use a mathematically linked pair, like a padlock anyone can snap shut but only one key opens.
KyberSlashThe 2023–24 timing attacks that recovered Kyber secret keys because a division instruction in reference code ran faster or slower depending on secret data. PQClean patched it — and it is why Phase 4 checks the decapsulation path rather than assuming it safe.
LatencyWaiting time: the delay between asking and receiving. Here, how long one cryptographic operation or one full handshake takes — measured in milliseconds (ms, thousandths of a second), microseconds (µs, millionths) or nanoseconds (ns, billionths).
LatticeAn endless regular grid of points, but in hundreds of dimensions. Finding special short vectors in such grids is believed hard even for quantum computers — the mathematical foundation under ML-KEM and ML-DSA.
MedianThe middle value when all samples are sorted. This project's headline statistic, because operating-system noise is one-sided — interruptions only ever add time — and the median resists those outliers where the mean is dragged upward (RSA keygen: median 62.2 ms, maximum 235 ms).
MicrocontrollerA tiny, cheap, low-power computer-on-a-chip — like the ARM Cortex-M4 modelled throughout § 8 — running at tens of MHz with kilobytes of memory. The brain of most IoT devices, thousands of times weaker than a laptop CPU.
NIST categoriesNIST's post-quantum security levels: categories 1/3/5 mean an attack must cost at least as much as key search on AES-128/192/256 respectively; category 2 matches collision search on SHA-256.
Nonce / freshnessA number used once. It makes each session or message unique, so yesterday's recorded traffic cannot be replayed as today's. The base paper binds timestamps into its session keys for the same reason; freshness is the property gained.
PQClean / pqm4PQClean is the reference collection of clean, portable-C post-quantum implementations; pqm4 is the community project that compiles and benchmarks that same source on a real Cortex-M4 chip. Together they form this project's same-codebase bridge from desktop to device.
PrimitiveA basic cryptographic building block — one algorithm doing one well-defined job, such as a cipher, a key exchange or a signature scheme. Complete systems (TLS, the base paper's framework, this project's handshake) are assembled from primitives.
ProtocolAn agreed sequence of messages two computers exchange — who sends what, in which order, verified how. The Phase 3 handshake is a four-message protocol; TLS is the internet's most-used one.
Public / private keyA matched pair at the heart of public-key cryptography: the public key may be shared with anyone (the open padlock); the private key stays secret (the only key that opens it). Anyone can lock a message to you; only you can unlock it.
Quantum computer / qubitA computer whose quantum bits (qubits) exploit superposition and interference to explore certain problems in fundamentally fewer steps. Not universally faster — but for factoring and discrete logarithms, Shor's algorithm makes the win total, which is the entire reason this field exists.
RFC 7228The IETF document classifying constrained devices by memory: Class 0 (≪10 kB RAM — too small for PQC alone), Class 1 (~10 kB — PQC only with care), Class 2 (~50 kB — can host a PQC stack). The scaffolding of § 8's recommendation matrix.
Session keyThe temporary symmetric key both sides derive during a handshake, use for that one conversation, and then discard. When it is derived from ephemeral exchanges, its disposability is what buys forward secrecy.
Shor / GroverThe two famous quantum algorithms. Shor breaks factoring and discrete logarithms in polynomial time — total defeat for RSA and elliptic curves. Grover searches any keyspace quadratically faster — merely halving symmetric key strength, which AES-256 absorbs.
Side channelInformation leaking through how a computation behaves — its timing, power draw or electromagnetic emissions — rather than through its official output. The safecracker who listens for clicks instead of trying every combination. Phase 4's subject.
SIKEAn isogeny-based NIST candidate with beautifully small keys, completely broken in 2022 by a classical attack after years of scrutiny. The cautionary tale motivating hybrid key exchange: confidence is not a guarantee.
SimulationA software model of a system — faithful only as far as its author's assumptions go. A model reproduces only what was put into it, which is why the base paper's simulated latencies needed checking against measured silicon (§ 8).
Standard deviationA measure of spread: how far individual samples typically sit from the average. Small means consistent timings; large means noise — or genuine variability, like ML-DSA's retrying signature loop. The z-scores of Phase 4 are counted in these units.
Symmetric cipherEncryption where both sides share one identical secret key — two copies of the same house key. Fast, compact, and quantum-resilient at 256-bit key sizes; its one weakness is needing the key agreed first, which is exactly the KEM's job.
TLSTransport Layer Security — the protocol behind the padlock icon in every browser. Its current version's deployed hybrid group X25519MLKEM768 is precisely the construction Phase 3 rebuilds and measures.
TranscriptThe exact byte-for-byte record of everything exchanged during a handshake. Hashing it into the key derivation binds the final key to the whole conversation, so any tampering en route produces mismatched keys and a handshake that fails closed.
